arxiv:2611.29064.abstract: Latent generative models typically rely on three separate networks: an encoder that tokenizes pixels, a generator that models the latent distribution, and a decoder that maps latents back to pixels. UNITE recently merged the first two into a single generative encoder trained in one stage, but its decoder remains a separate network. We ask whether this last network can be folded in too, so that one diffusion transformer encodes, generates, and decodes. Simply letting the shared backbone decode does not help. What makes it work is to cast all three modes as position-aligned sequence maps over one fully shared backbone, distinguished only by a mode token and the timestep. The resulting model, UNIFIED, is simple: one network trained from scratch in a single stage with only reconstruction and flow-matching losses, without adversarial losses or pretrained encoders (e.g., DINO). On ImageNet-1K 256x256 at matched parameters, UNIFIED improves gFID over UNITE at three sizes (~60M, ~115M, and ~215M) and reaches 2.08 with 215M parameters, the lowest among compared models under 250M parameters. On text-to-image generation, UNIFIED-B (218M) reaches a GenEval score of 0.87 at 512x512, exceeding single-stage pixel diffusion models with around one billion parameters. Full unification of latent diffusion is thus not merely feasible but beneficial.
arxiv:2611.29064.authors: Hao-Yu Hsu, Shenlong Wang, Alexander G. Schwing

arxiv:2611.29723.title: ApexID: Hierarchical Learning for Multi-Species Animal Re-Identification
arxiv:2611.29723.abstract: Animal re-identification (Re-ID) must distinguish individuals across species and capture conditions. We introduce ApexID, a hierarchical SphereFace2-based loss that integrates global identity discrimination with balanced animal-category supervision. Using 132,533 images curated from 19 public datasets, we evaluate three model families and four objectives on four external datasets with observation-aware retrieval protocols. ApexID achieves a dataset-averaged Rank-1 accuracy of 64.89% with ConvNeXt-Small and an mAP of 32.54% with MIEW-ID, outperforming their pretrained reference models. On elephants, a category absent from animal Re-ID training, our ConvNeXt-Small variant achieves the highest retrieval performance among the fourteen evaluated configurations. Scores vary by backbone and dataset, and open-set evaluation reveals remaining discovery challenges. These findings support hierarchical category-identity learning to improve transfer to unseen datasets and species.
arxiv:2611.29723.authors: Seifeldin Elkerdany, Mohamed ElBassat, Gamal Abouelhamd, Assem Elkady, Jana Ghoneim, Matin Mahmood, Abigail Allen Martin, Gerard de Melo, Antonio Rueda-Toicen

arxiv:2611.26863.title: LLMs Memorize Their Own Hallucinations During Post-Training
arxiv:2611.26863.abstract: Reasoning domains have shaped the post-training recipes of frontier models even though they are trained and deployed in domains beyond math and code. In this paper, we study the consequences of directly adopting reasoning-centric training recipes, e.g., the use of outcome-based rewards for reinforcement learning (RL), injection of "cognitive" behaviors such as proposing and backtracking from hypotheses in reasoning chains, etc., for knowledge tasks. We hypothesize that these decisions, while useful for reasoning, inadvertently encourage models to memorize hallucinations they themselves generate in their long reasoning chains when trained on knowledge tasks. To study this, we train models with standard post-training, extract their self-generated hallucinations during RL, and track memorization throughout the rest of training. Our experiments on six open models across two model families and two architectures confirm our hypothesis. We find that models' recall of hallucinations reinforced during training increases by 4.83% on average, compared to just 0.17% for self-hallucinations that receive no training signal. In fact, models even memorize false facts that they immediately retract in their reasoning; a backtracking template inherited from reasoning-centric training that has no benefit for knowledge recall. Furthermore, we find that memorization is strongest on the hardest training questions, and rewarding a hallucination makes the model less likely to abstain from it later (by 7.23% on average). Overall, our work identifies and systematically studies a previously unexamined pathway through which models learn hallucinations during training.

arxiv:2611.31198.title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents
arxiv:2611.31198.abstract: Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.
arxiv:2611.31198.authors: Rui Sun, Junhua Huang, Luca Zancato, Md Mofijul Islam, Kai-Wei Chang

arxiv:2611.30495.title: DexDuet: Learning Contact-Preserving Bimanual Dexterity from Human Demonstrations
arxiv:2611.30495.abstract: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/
arxiv:2611.30495.authors: Haoran Zhang, Haokai Ding, Han Zhou, Zuxing Lu, Heng Zhang, Xingxing Zuo

arxiv:2611.28489.title: Open Vision Banana: An Open Framework for Unified Visual Perception through Generation in RGB Space
arxiv:2611.28489.abstract: Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to \emph{open} generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with \textbf{Open Vision Banana (OVB)}, an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a \emph{task contract} whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 $δ_1$ stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned $δ_1$ wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned $δ_1$ from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman $ρ\approx-0.9$ between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.
arxiv:2611.28489.authors: Xu Lin, Ruilin Yao, Haoran Xu, Zixiang Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Zhao, Pu Miao, Chonghan Liu

arxiv:2611.29619.title: Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge
arxiv:2611.29619.abstract: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.
arxiv:2611.29619.authors: Panagiotis Kasnesis, Lazaros Toumanidis, Amalia Contiero Syropoulou, Christos Chatzigeorgiou

arxiv:2611.31053.title: ReWeave: Emergent Physical Task Topologies for Embodied Harness Optimization and Cross-Task Meta-Distillation
arxiv:2611.31053.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks involve physical dependencies that may only become clear through interaction. As task understanding deepens, past trials can reveal new information for adaptation and transfer. However, coarse progress feedback cannot identify which physical preconditions held, leaving search unguided, while task-specific optimization easily overfits to individual scenes, making cross-task transfer brittle. We introduce ReWeave, a framework that jointly optimizes an embodied agent harness and an emergent physical task topology from interaction without updating policy weights. Keeping execution policies and perception frozen, ReWeave co-optimizes coupled context, workflows, and control loops. As new evidence revises the topology, ReWeave reprojects past trials onto the updated task understanding, exposing retained progress, regressions, and bottlenecks that guide parent selection and search width. Across tasks, matching verified local mechanisms to unmet preconditions consolidates 72 specialist units into 44 reusable groups ($0.34\times$ full concatenation) within a compact shared harness capable of continual learning. ReWeave improves held-out success from 89.00% to 98.75% on LIBERO-PRO and from 25.50% to 58.25% on RoboDojo, while uncovering retained progress in 89% of 159 failed RoboDojo development trials and translating stronger offline reasoning into higher online performance. On eight unseen LIBERO-PRO tasks, the shared harness reaches 51.3% success versus 41.3% for direct distillation, rising to 75.0% after continual learning.
arxiv:2611.31053.authors: Yicheng Xu, Wencan Jiang, Zihao Zhu, Keru Zhou, Chang Zhou, Li Liu, Maoqing Yao, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang

arxiv:2611.30011.title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
arxiv:2611.30011.abstract: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.
arxiv:2611.30011.authors: Ce Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Jinxi He, Xiyuan Yang, Pan Wang, Han Liu, Katia Sycara, Yaqi Xie

arxiv:2611.30627.title: From Rewarding What Models Say to How They Think: Attention Process Reward Model for LLM Reinforcement Learning
arxiv:2611.30627.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture high-quality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88\%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.
arxiv:2611.30627.authors: Kairong Han, Nuanqiao Shan, Ziyu Zhao, Xinpeng Dong, Zijing Hu, Dian Jin, Leyan Deng, Junjian Ye, Lujia Pan, Fei Wu, Kun Kuang

arxiv:2611.30597.title: ViDiHand2: Unifying Video Diffusion Priors and Hand Geometry for 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild
arxiv:2611.30597.abstract: Learning robot manipulation from egocentric human videos requires accurate metric 3D hand motion. Recent methods leverage pretrained video diffusion model (VDM) priors to recover occluded hands directly from full-frame videos, but their appearance-based depth regression generalizes poorly to unseen cameras. In this work, we propose ViDiHand2, a geometry-driven framework that reformulates VDM-based hand depth estimation from direct regression into fine-grained geometric constraint solving. Specifically, we introduce Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting and Clip-Level Ray Fitting, which recover metric depth by enforcing geometric consistency between pixel-aligned 2D joints and the metric structure of MANO hands, while leveraging temporal observations across the clip. Since the lifting relies on these 2D joints, to improve robustness under occlusion and image truncation, we further develop Confidence-Gated Fusion to adaptively combine geometrically lifted joints with MANO predictions according to localization confidence. Finally, we enhance the VDM backbone to better capture spatial-temporal representations and produce the per-frame 2D joint and MANO predictions that both steps rely on. Extensive experiments on seven public datasets demonstrate that ViDiHand2 consistently outperforms 18 baselines, reducing in-the-wild absolute joint error by 42% and detection failures by 8.82x compared with the best baseline on each metric, while running at 57 FPS. The code is available at https://github.com/NTUYWANG103/ViDiHand.
arxiv:2611.30597.authors: Yuxi Wang, Yufei Liu, Chengkai Jin, Qingyue Chen, Wenqi Ouyang, Tianyi Wei, Kerui Ren, Siyuan Huang, Zhiqi Shen, Hongsheng Li, Xingang Pan

arxiv:2611.30287.title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation
arxiv:2611.30287.abstract: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.
arxiv:2611.30287.authors: Yuxuan Chen, Changwei Lv, Yunfei Li, Zhongjing Du, Kehui Tan, Zijun Liao, Ruochong Zheng, Hao Chen, Can Deng, Zheni Zeng, Chang Liu, Jie Chen

arxiv:2611.30157.title: UUBench: Understanding the Unspoken toward Full-Duplex Multimodal Interaction
arxiv:2611.30157.abstract: Effective real-time, full-duplex multimodal interaction requires systems to understand not only what users say, but also the communicative needs conveyed through prosody, facial expressions, gestures, and context, and to generate audiovisual responses that appropriately address those needs. Existing evaluations offer limited insight into whether systems translate an understanding of such unspoken needs into effective responses. We introduce UUBench, a benchmark for assessing how well multimodal interactive systems Understand the Unspoken intent and address users' implicit communicative needs. The inherent subjectivity of implicit intent inference poses a key challenge for evaluation. To address this, we introduce Process-Oriented Scoring, which grounds the assessment of intent fulfillment in observable auditory and visual cues, such as prosody and gestures. Rather than relying solely on a single overall score, it evaluates how well a response addresses the communicative needs conveyed by each applicable primitive dimension. We aggregate the dimension-level scores according to each dimension's relevance to the annotated evidence. Beyond intent fulfillment, Outcome-Oriented Scoring evaluates the naturalness, appropriateness, and human-likeness of the reply itself under audio-only, visual-only, and audiovisual conditions. To make these judgments traceable to observable evidence, we propose a Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV module, which uses structured, timestamped audiovisual observations of the user and the digital human's reply to assess one dimension or criterion at a time. UUBench provides a foundation for assessing whether multimodal interactive systems respond effectively to meaning beyond literal wording, supporting progress toward context-aware, real-time, full-duplex interaction.
arxiv:2611.30157.authors: Ye Pan, Chenfei Liao, Bin Ren, Hanqian Li, Haocong He, Jialei Chen, Jinlin He, Kunyu Peng, Mengyu Jin, Shijie Li, Wenqian Cui, Yuanqi Yao, Yuqian Fu, Kailong Ruan, Yuan Gao, Wei Wang, Xuming Hu, Irwin King, Nicu Sebe, Xu Zheng

arxiv:2611.30662.title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce
arxiv:2611.30662.abstract: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.
arxiv:2611.30662.authors: Binhui Xie, Jinmin Li, Haomiao Tang, Guangting Wang, Song Jin, Jianwei Zhu, Fengyun Rao, Jing Lyu

arxiv:2611.29006.title: NoHairCache: Calibrate-Once KV Cache Eviction with One Power-Law Exponent
arxiv:2611.29006.abstract: The decay exponent $α$ in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as $s_i = A_i \cdot (t-i)^{-α}$, where $A_i$ is cumulative attention and $α$ controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to $α=0$ and $α\to\infty$, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch).   The no-hair mechanism of \citet{xiang2026nohair} bounds the admissible range of $α$, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields $[0.556, 0.822]$ for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps.   \textsc{NoHairCache} achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM ($p < 0.05$ on all three datasets, with $0.06$--$0.10$ PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget $512$). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining $98.2\%$ of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at $25\%$ retention versus $91.1\%$ for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.

arxiv:2611.28227.title: Feedback Shortcut: Speculative Decoding for Latent Feedback Transformers
arxiv:2611.28227.abstract: Feeding each position's top-layer hidden state back into the next position's input improves Transformer performance. However, this feedback breaks speculative decoding, since verifying a drafted token requires the top-layer state from its preceding position, which forces the draft to rely on an approximate stand-in. Training the model to adapt to this stand-in can lower the exact-decoding performance ceiling, while using it at inference time further introduces approximation error. We propose Feedback Shortcut to address both bottlenecks. First, state alignment trains a lightweight projection from multi-token prediction head states to stand-ins, leaving base model training untouched. Second, pipelined correction re-evaluates each draft using its predecessor's newly computed state, a much closer proxy to true feedback. Running this correction inside the verification pass of subsequent drafts improves accuracy with zero extra calls. Across 135M and 780M scales, Feedback Shortcut stays within $10^{-4}$ bits per byte of the exact-decoding ceiling on Paloma and accelerates decoding by 2.4-2.8x with about 2% more training compute than the latent feedback Transformer. At large batch sizes, skipping correction still preserves Transformer speed and over 80% of latent feedback's gains.
arxiv:2611.28227.authors: Benhao Huang, Xuezhe Ma, Hector Liu

arxiv:2611.29355.title: Polytropos: What Do Vision-Language Model Descriptions Make of a Cultural Object?
arxiv:2611.29355.abstract: Vision-language models have become a new kind of describer, writing about almost anything people see, and their descriptions now shape how cultures are known by people and by other models. Descriptions of cultures tend to turn particular things into types, and what a description loses shows what its describer lacks. We introduce Polytropos, a benchmark that measures what model descriptions of cultural objects keep of the particular object by turning each description back into an image and comparing it with the original photograph. On 374 objects from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Getty, with 1,870 descriptions from five models and 230 written by curators, reconstructions are recognised as the recorded culture more often than the photographs, at 54.55% to 59.09% against 52.14%, yet 16% to 21% of objects change outcome and only 0.49% of reconstructions are identified as the specific object. On the same objects, models lose recorded cultures at a rate similar to curators but gain more. Model descriptions give each object many faces, each typical of its culture and almost none the object itself.
arxiv:2611.29355.authors: Yuechen Jiang, Enze Zhang, Yuyan Wang, Mohsinul Kabir, Chenying Lin, Sijia Li, Qianqian Xie, Stavroula Golfomitsou, Konstantinos Arvanitis, Sophia Ananiadou

arxiv:2611.26389.title: ViDecide: Teaching Video Diffusion Models to Reason and Plan Step by Step
arxiv:2611.26389.abstract: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of decisions. We present ViDecide, a decision-centric framework that trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop, with a decision-focused training schedule. We further propose Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), which corrects failed decisions by mapping their noise to the model's own successful continuations, achieving stable improvement without policy-gradient optimization. Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a new benchmark of multi-step robot planning, ViDecide achieves an average strict success rate of 83.8%, far above 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Our framework therefore unlocks greater potential for video generation models as reliable reasoners and planners in the visual world. Project page: https://kevin-thu.github.io/ViDecide.
arxiv:2611.26389.authors: Kaiwen Zhang, Yiming Gao, Zeqi Xiao, Xintao Wang, Pengfei Wan, Kun Gai, Xingang Pan

arxiv:2611.29473.title: The norm axiom and factor hyperfields
arxiv:2611.29473.abstract: Touchard and the author asked whether every valued hyperfield, in Krasner's sense with the norm axiom, is of the form $\mathcal{H}_ρ(K)$: a valued field $K$ read up to relative error $ρ$. The question turns on the norm axiom. If a valued hyperfield is a quotient $K^\times/T\cup\{0\}$ of a field, the norm axiom forces $T=1+\mathfrak{m}_ρ$ for a valuation on $K$. This completes the proof of a published proposition, and it makes the question equivalent to asking whether every Krasner valued hyperfield is such a quotient. For value group $\mathbb{Z}$ we prove directly that it is. Without the norm axiom the answer is negative. Layering a hyperfield over a non-trivial ordered abelian group gives a factor hyperfield exactly when the hyperfield itself is one, so Massouros's hyperfields yield hyperfields with a non-trivial valuation, satisfying all the other axioms, that are not factor hyperfields. The general question remains open.

arxiv:2611.27376.title: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training
arxiv:2611.27376.abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.
arxiv:2611.27376.authors: Zhen Zhang, Changyi Yang, Xuehai He, Chengzhi Liu, Yutong Yin, Ziyue Liu, Zhuoran Yin, Yangmin Li, Zhihan Liu, Jisen Li, Mingyu Jin, Chuhan Li, Zhaotian Weng, Ruoyu He, Wenyao Gao, Jiaxin Deng, Chenwei Wu, Hui Shen, Wenhao Chai, Chenyang Zhao, Zhuofan Ying, Kieran Liu, Andrew Chen, Pony Ma, Zhaoran Wang, Alkesh Patel, Zhe Gan, Xin Eric Wang

arxiv:2611.26254.title: Prism: Hierarchical Text Detection with Minimalist Design
arxiv:2611.26254.abstract: Hierarchical text detection aims to localize words, text lines, and paragraphs while parsing their structural relationships. It provides essential structural cues for visual text understanding. To maximize accuracy, existing methods typically rely on complex multi-scale feature fusion necks and heavy-weight heads, resulting in bloated architectures and low inference efficiency. In this paper, we argue that a sufficiently pre-trained backbone can effectively replace these sophisticated external modules, while simple geometric inclusion suffices for hierarchical text structural parsing. Thus, we propose Prism, a minimalist framework for hierarchical text detection. Prism performs multi-granularity detection by attaching parallel lightweight heads to a single-scale backbone feature map, covering words, text lines, and paragraphs, and reconstructs the structural hierarchy via an efficient geometric inclusion algorithm. In addition, we systematically compare representative lightweight head archetypes and show that pixel-level regression offers the best accuracy-efficiency trade-off in this setting. Experiments on multiple public benchmarks show that our significantly simplified architecture achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkable efficiency. Specifically, it runs $1.7\times$ faster than LRANet on CTW1500 while achieving higher accuracy, and surpasses the current SOTA method, OmniParser V2, by over 6 PQ points on the hierarchical HierText dataset. Code will be released soon.
arxiv:2611.26254.authors: Yuchen Su, Xuesheng Wang, Zhilong Ji, Jinfeng Bai, Shijian Lu, Zhineng Chen

arxiv:2611.28665.title: Seeing Right, Writing Wrong: Where Short Chain-of-Thought Breaks Spatial VQA
arxiv:2611.28665.abstract: Asking a vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns a perception problem into a transcription problem. Once a VLM writes a spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. Studying 15 open VLMs (2B-38B) and six frontier closed models, we rule out token count, turn format, and visual forgetting in open models and trace the failure through three stages. First, writing re-weights visual cues, weakening a "lower is closer" shortcut in all 13 open models tested but also discarding valid cues, which produces false relations. Second, the written text takes over. With the model's own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed, swapping in an opposite-depth image moves the answer by 2-9 points on rendered twins (vs. up to 77 for direct answers) and by 3.0-3.4 points on average on natural photographs (vs. 20.5-69.6). Third, the concluding sentence can invert even a true relation, mainly on converse questions. Together, false relations and conclusion mis-mapping account for four in five CoT losses. Scale does not remove this bottleneck: Qwen3-VL-32B shows the same pattern. Frontier closed models are not hurt: they write relations as accurately as they answer, and three of six re-check the image after writing. The three queried with reasoning off lock in like open models, so re-grounding co-occurs with answer-turn reasoning; we identify answer-step re-grounding as the step open VLMs lack. In a single-model pilot, fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels restores it on natural photographs. We open-sourced all our datasets and code at https://ming-zch.github.io/seeing-right-writing-wrong.

arxiv:2611.30235.title: PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding
arxiv:2611.30235.abstract: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy, the highest among the evaluated single-forward grounders, with a mean latency of 0.43 s per target.
arxiv:2611.30235.authors: Kanghui Tian, Shuai Dong, Yuhan Zhu, Congcong Wang, Ji Zhao, Tianxiang Jiang, Zhixiong Zhang, Shengyuan Ding, Yi Wang, Jiaqi Wang, Yu Qiao

rss:2026-p001.title: One-Shot Real-World Demonstration Synthesis for Scalable Bimanual Manipulation
rss:2026-p001.abstract: Learning dexterous bimanual manipulation policies critically depends on large-scale, high-quality demonstrations, yet current paradigms face inherent trade-offs: teleoperation provides physically grounded data but is prohibitively labor-intensive, while simulation-based synthesis scales efficiently but suffers from sim-to-real gaps. We present BiDemoSyn, a framework that synthesizes contact-rich, physically feasible bimanual demonstrations from a single real-world example. The key idea is to decompose tasks into invariant coordination blocks and variable, object-dependent adjustments, then adapt them through vision-guided alignment and lightweight trajectory optimization. This enables the generation of thousands of diverse and feasible demonstrations within several hour, without repeated teleoperation or reliance on imperfect simulation. Across six dual-arm tasks, we show that policies trained on BiDemoSyn data generalize robustly to novel object poses and shapes, significantly outperforming recent strong baselines. Beyond the one-shot setting, BiDemoSyn naturally extends to few-shot-based synthesis, improving object-level diversity and out-of-distribution generalization while maintaining strong data efficiency. Moreover, policies trained on BiDemoSyn data exhibit zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer to new robotic platforms, enabled by object-centric observations and a simplified 6-DoF end-effector action representation that decouples policies from embodiment-specific dynamics. By bridging the gap between efficiency and real-world fidelity, BiDemoSyn provides a scalable path toward practical imitation learning for complex bimanual manipulation without compromising physical grounding.

rss:2026-p002.title: Supervised Mixture-of-Experts for Surgical Grasping and Retraction
rss:2026-p002.abstract: Imitation learning has achieved remarkable success in robotic manipulation, yet its application to surgical robotics remains challenging due to data scarcity, constrained workspaces, and the need for an exceptional level of safety and predictability. We present a supervised Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture designed for phase-structured surgical manipulation tasks, which can be added on top of any autonomous policy. Unlike prior surgical robot learning approaches that rely on multi-camera setups or thousands of demonstrations, we show that a lightweight action decoder policy like Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) can learn complex, long-horizon manipulation from less than 150 demonstrations using solely stereo endoscopic images, when equipped with our architecture. We evaluate our approach on the collaborative surgical task of bowel grasping and retraction, where a robot assistant interprets visual cues from a human surgeon, executes targeted grasping on deformable tissue, and performs sustained retraction. We benchmark our method against state-of-the-art Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and the standard ACT baseline. Our results show that generalist VLAs fail to acquire the task entirely, even under standard in-distribution conditions. Furthermore, while standard ACT achieves moderate success in-distribution, adopting a supervised MoE architecture significantly boosts its performance, yielding higher success rates in-distribution and demonstrating superior robustness in out-of-distribution scenarios, including novel grasp locations, reduced illumination, and partial occlusions. Notably, it generalizes to unseen testing viewpoints and also transfers zero-shot to ex vivo porcine tissue without additional training, offering a promising pathway toward in vivo deployment. To support this statement, we present qualitative preliminary results of policy roll-outs during in vivo porcine surgery. These results demonstrate that supervised MoE architectures provide a data-efficient approach for learning multi-step dexterous manipulation in visually constrained environments. Code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.

rss:2026-p003.title: DexImit: Learning Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation from Monocular Human Videos
rss:2026-p003.abstract: Data scarcity fundamentally limits the generalization of bimanual dexterous manipulation, as real-world data collection for dexterous hands is expensive and labor-intensive. Human manipulation videos, as a direct carrier of manipulation knowledge, offer significant potential for scaling up robot learning. However, the substantial embodiment gap between human hands and robotic dexterous hands makes direct pretraining from human videos extremely challenging. To bridge this gap and unleash the potential of large-scale human manipulation video data, we propose DexImit, an automated framework that converts monocular human manipulation videos into physically plausible robot data, without any additional information. DexImit employs a four-stage generation pipeline: (1) reconstructing handâobject interactions from arbitrary viewpoints with near-metric scale; (2) performing subtask decomposition and bimanual scheduling; (3) synthesizing robot trajectories consistent with the demonstrated interactions; (4) comprehensive data augmentation for zero-shot real-world deployment. Building on these designs, DexImit can generate large-scale robot data based on human videos, either from the Internet or video generation models. DexImit is capable of handling diverse manipulation tasks, including tool use (e.g., cutting an apple), long-horizon tasks (e.g., making a beverage), and fine-grained manipulations (e.g., stacking cups).
rss:2026-p003.authors: Juncheng Mu, Sizhe Yang, Yiming Bao, Hojin Bae, Tianming Wei, Linning Xu, Boyi Li, Huazhe Xu, Jiangmiao Pang

rss:2026-p004.title: Semantic Contact Fields for Category-Level Generalizable Tool Manipulation
rss:2026-p004.abstract: Generalizing tool manipulation requires both semantic planning and precise physical control. Modern generalist robot policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, often lack the high-fidelity physical grounding required for contact-rich tool manipulation. Conversely, existing contact-aware policies that leverage tactile or haptic sensing are typically instance-specific and fail to generalize across diverse tool geometries. Bridging this gap requires learning unified contact representations from diverse data, yet a fundamental barrier remains: diverse real-world tactile data are prohibitive at scale, while direct zero-shot sim-to-real transfer is challenging due to the complex dynamics of nonlinear deformation of soft sensors. To address this, we propose Semantic-Contact Fields (SCFields), a unified 3D representation fusing visual semantics with dense contact estimates. We enable this via a two-stage Sim-to-Real Contact Learning Pipeline: first, we pre-train on a large simulation data set to learn general contact physics; second, we fine-tune on a small set of real data, pseudo-labeled via geometric heuristics and force optimization, to align sensor characteristics. This allows physical generalization to unseen tools. We leverage SCFields as the dense observation input for a diffusion policy to enable robust execution of contact-rich tool manipulation tasks. Experiments on scraping, crayon drawing, and peeling demonstrate robust category-level generalization, significantly outperforming vision-only and raw-tactile baselines.
rss:2026-p004.authors: Kevin Yuchen Ma, Heng Zhang, Weisi Lin, Mike Zheng Shou, Yan Wu

rss:2026-p005.title: Contact-Grounded Policy: Dexterous Visuotactile Policy with Generative Contact Grounding
rss:2026-p005.abstract: Contact-rich dexterous manipulation with multi-finger hands remains an open challenge in robotics because task success depends on multi-point contacts that continuously evolve and are highly sensitive to object geometry, frictional transitions, and slip. Recently, tactile-informed manipulation policies have shown promise. However, most use tactile signals as additional observations rather than modeling contact state or how their action outputs interact with low-level controller dynamics. We present Contact-Grounded Policy (CGP), a visuotactile policy that grounds multi-point contacts by predicting coupled trajectories of actual robot state and tactile feedback, and using a learned contact-consistency mapping to convert these predictions into executable target robot states for a compliance controller. CGP consists of two components: (i) a conditional diffusion model that forecasts future robot state and tactile feedback in a compressed latent space, and (ii) a learned contact-consistency mapping that converts the predicted robot state-tactile pair into executable targets for a compliance controller, enabling it to realize the intended contacts. We evaluate CGP using a physical four-finger Allegro V5 hand with Digit360 fingertip tactile sensors, and a simulated five-finger Tesollo DG-5F hand with dense whole-hand tactile arrays. Across a range of dexterous tasks including in-hand manipulation, delicate grasping, and tool use, CGP outperforms visuomotor and visuotactile diffusion-policy baselines.
rss:2026-p005.authors: Zhengtong Xu, Yeping Wang, Ben Abbatematteo, Jom Preechayasomboon, Sonny Chan, Nicholas Colonnese, Amirhossein H. Memar

rss:2026-p006.title: TactAlign: Human-to-Robot Policy Transfer via Tactile Alignment
rss:2026-p006.abstract: Human demonstrations collected by wearable devices (e.g., tactile gloves) provide fast and dexterous supervision for policy learning, and are guided by rich, natural tactile feedback. However, a key challenge is how to transfer human-collected tactile signals to robots despite the differences in sensing modalities and embodiment. Existing human-to-robot (H2R) approaches that incorporate touch often assume identical tactile sensors, require paired data, and involve little to no embodiment gap between human demonstrator and the robots, limiting scalability and generality. We propose TactAlign, a cross-embodiment tactile alignment method that transfers human-collected tactile signals to a robot with different embodiment. TactAlign transforms human and robot tactile observations into an shared latent representation using a rectified flow, without paired datasets, manual labels, or privileged information. Our method enables low-cost latent transport guided by hand-object interaction-derived pseudo-pairs. We demonstrate that TactAlign improves H2R policy transfer across multiple contact-rich tasks (pivoting, insertion, lid closing), generalizes to unseen objects and tasks with human data (approximately 5 minutes), and enables zero-shot H2R transfer on a highly dexterous tasks (light bulb screwing).
rss:2026-p006.authors: Youngsun Wi, Jessica Yin, Elvis Xiang, Akash Sharma, Jitendra Malik, Mustafa Mukadam, Nima Fazeli, Tess Hellebrekers

rss:2026-p007.title: A Systematic Study of Data Modalities and Strategies for Co-training Large Behavior Models for Robot Manipulation
rss:2026-p007.abstract: Large behavior models (LBMs) have shown strong dexterous manipulation capabilities by extending imitation learning to large-scale training on extensive multi-task robot data, yet their generalization remains limited by the insufficient coverage of available robot data. To expand this coverage without costly additional data collection, recent work increasingly relies on co-training: jointly learning from target robot data and heterogeneous data modalities. However, how different co-training data modalities and training strategies affect policy performance remains poorly understood. We present a large-scale empirical study examining five co-training data modalities---standard vision-language data, dense language annotations for robot trajectories, cross-embodiment robot data, human videos, and discrete robot action tokensâacross single- and multi-phase training strategies. Our study leverages 4,000 hours of robot and human manipulation data and 50M visionâlanguage samples to train vision-language-action (VLA) policies. We evaluate 89 policies over 58,000 simulation rollouts and 2,835 real-world rollouts. Our results show that co-training with various forms of vision-language and cross-embodiment robot data substantially improves generalization to distribution shifts, unseen tasks, and language following, while discrete action token variants yield no statistically significant benefits. Furthermore, combining effective modalities produces cumulative gains and enables rapid adaptation to unseen long-horizon dexterous tasks via fine-tuning. Together, these results provide a systematic understanding of co-training and practical guidance for building scalable generalist robot policies.
rss:2026-p007.authors: Fanqi Lin, Kushal Arora, Jean Mercat, Haruki Nishimura, Paarth Shah, Chen Xu, Mengchao Zhang, Mark Zolotas, Maya Angeles, Owen Pfannenstiehl, Andrew Beaulieu, Jose Barreiros

rss:2026-p008.title: SID: Sliding into Distribution for Robust Few-Demonstration Manipulation
rss:2026-p008.abstract: Generalizing robotic manipulation across object poses, viewpoints, and dynamic disturbances is difficult, especially with only a few demonstrations. End-to-end visuomotor policies are expressive but data-hungry, while planning and optimization satisfy explicit constraints but do not directly capture the interaction strategies demonstrated by humans. We propose *Sliding into Distribution* (SID), a structured framework that learns an object-centric motion field from canonicalized demonstrations to iteratively *slide* the system toward the demonstrated manifold and into the reliable operating region of a lightweight egocentric execution policy, mitigating out-of-distribution (OOD) execution. The motion field provides large corrective motions when far from the demonstration manifold and naturally vanishes near convergence, enabling robust reaching under substantial pose and viewpoint shifts. Within the reached regime, an egocentric policy trained with conditioned flow matching performs task-specific manipulation, supported by kinematically consistent point-cloud reprojection augmentation that preserves action--observation consistency. Across six real-world tasks, SID achieves approximately 90% success under OOD initializations with only two demonstrations, with under a 10% drop under distractors and external disturbances. Overall, SID provides a new paradigm for few-shot manipulation: explicitly managing distribution shift via online distribution recovery.
rss:2026-p008.authors: Yicheng Ma, Wei Yu, Zhian Su, Xidan Zhang, Huixu Dong

rss:2026-p009.title: UMI-Underwater: Learning Underwater Manipulation without Underwater Teleoperation
rss:2026-p009.abstract: Underwater robotic grasping is difficult due to degraded, highly variable imagery and the expense of collecting diverse underwater demonstrations. We introduce a system that (i) autonomously collects successful underwater grasp demonstrations via a self-supervised data collection pipeline and (ii) transfers grasp knowledge from on-land human demonstrations through a depth-based affordance representation that bridges the on-landâtoâunderwater domain gap and is robust to lighting and color shift. An affordance model trained on on-land handheld demonstrations is deployed underwater zero-shot via geometric alignment, and an affordance-conditioned diffusion policy is then trained on underwater demonstrations to generate control actions. In pool experiments, our approach improves grasping performance and robustness to background shifts, and enables generalization to objects seen only in on-land data, outperforming RGB-only baselines.
rss:2026-p009.authors: Hao Li, Long Yin Chung, Jack Goler, Ryan Zhang, Xiaochi Xie, Huy Ha, Shuran Song, Mark Cutkosky

rss:2026-p010.title: Memory Retrieval in Visuomotor Policies for Long-Horizon Robot Control
rss:2026-p010.abstract: General-purpose robots operating in partially observable environments such as homes require memory to support long-term autonomy. They must recall different types of past information, such as where objects were placed, which subtasks have already been completed by a human partner, and when an appliance was turned on This capability requires an effective memory retrieval mechanism. However, hand-designed or heuristic-based retrieval methods often fail to generalize in different tasks. Attention-based retrieval provides a promising alternative, as both queries and keys are learned from data without making task-specific assumptions. However, directly applying an attention-based memory retrieval mechanism in imitation learning introduces two key challenges: (1) the policy may learn spurious correlations between the information retrieved from the past and predicted actions, and (2) errors accumulated over time in the memory due to prediction inaccuracies, compounded by interactions with the environment, lead to model drift and cascading failures in long-horizon control. To address these challenges, we introduce HALO, a visuomotor policy equipped with an attention-based memory retrieval mechanism for long-horizon control. To mitigate spurious correlations, HALO leverages vision-language models (VLMs) by generating task-relevant questionâanswer pairs from demonstration trajectories and jointly training the policy with a video questionâ answering objective. This supervision encourages the retrieval module to focus on information that is relevant to the task. Second, to reduce the impact of accumulated errors in memory during closed-loop control, HALO uses sparse attention that restricts retrieval to only the most relevant parts of the history. Together, these components enable more reliable long-horizon control by guiding the policy to retrieve task-relevant information from up to two minutes of past experience.
rss:2026-p010.authors: Rutav Shah, Yisu Li, Femi Bello, Yuke Zhu, Roberto MartÃ­n-MartÃ­n

rss:2026-p011.title: RAG-Diff: Adapting Diffusion Policies to Dynamic Constraints with Retrieval-Augmented Guidance
rss:2026-p011.abstract: Robots operating in unstructured environments must satisfy dynamic constraints that can change across tasks and even within a single execution. While diffusion policies can learn multimodal behaviors from demonstrations, adapting a trained policy at runtime to newly encountered or evolving constraints remains an open challenge. We propose RAG-Diff, a runtime adaptation framework for a frozen transformer diffusion policy that leverages retrieval-augmented memory. RAG-Diff maintains PrefMem, a memory bank that stores vision-language embeddings together with (i) state-action snippets and (ii) constraint annotations. At test time, RAG-Diff queries PrefMem to retrieve the nearest entry and uses it to steer sampling in two complementary ways. First, I-Atten (in-place attention recomputation) inserts the retrieved snippet as additional cross-attention memory tokens and performs a classifier-free-guidance-style update, biasing denoising toward preference-consistent motion. Second, a predictive guidance mechanism incorporates the retrieved constraint parameters during diffusion sampling to discourage violations. To demonstrate the effectiveness of RAG-Diff, we choose physical robot caregiving as a domain with personalized and time-varying constraints. We first benchmark on an adapted PushT environment in simulation with contact-force limits and region-to-avoid constraints. We then evaluated our method on a suite of physical caregiving tasks spanning diverse preference types: (i) interaction and affordance preferences in bed bathing, (ii) ROM-based assistance-level preferences in medicine delivery, (iii) semantic preferences in shelf cleaning, and (iv) trajectory preferences in feeding, in both RCareWorld simulation and with a real robot. We further conducted real-world user studies on the bed-bathing task. Results show that RAG-Diff improves both task success and constraint satisfaction compared to a range of baselines, including unguided diffusion and other guidance- or sampling-based variants.
rss:2026-p011.authors: Ruolin Ye, Nayoung Ha, Shuaixing Chen, Qiandao Liu, Gavin Chen, Shaoyang Stassen, Mark Zolotas, Jose Barreiros, Tapomayukh Bhattacharjee

rss:2026-p012.title: Self-Improving Robot Policy with Compositional World Model
rss:2026-p012.abstract: Despite the sustained scaling on model capacity and data acquisition, VisionâLanguageâAction (VLA) models remain brittle in contact-rich and dynamic manipulation tasks, where minor execution deviations can compound into failures. While reinforcement learning (RL) offers a principled path to robustness, on-policy RL in the physical world is constrained by safety risk, hardware cost, and environment reset. To bridge this gap, we present RISE, a scalable framework of robotic reinforcement learning via imagination. At its core is a Compositional World Model that (i) predicts multi-view future via a controllable dynamics model, and (ii) evaluates imagined outcomes with a progress value model, producing informative advantages for the policy improvement. Such compositional design enables state and value to be modeled by best-suited yet distinct architectures and objectives. These components are integrated into a closed-loop self-improving pipeline that continuously generates imaginary rollouts, estimates advantages, and updates the policy in imaginary space without costly physical interaction. Across three challenging real-world tasks, RISE yields significant improvement over prior art, with more than +35% absolute performance increase in dynamic brick sorting, +45% for backpack packing, and +35% for box closing, respectively.
rss:2026-p012.authors: Jiazhi Yang, Kunyang Lin, Wencong Zhang, Jinwei Li, Tianwei Lin, Longyan Wu, Ya-Qin Zhang, Hao Zhao, Ping Luo, Zhizhong Su, Hongyang Li, Xiangyu Yue, Li Chen

rss:2026-p013.title: HAIC: Humanoid Agile Object Interaction Control via Dynamics-Aware World Model
rss:2026-p013.abstract: Humanoid robots exhibit significant potential for executing complex whole-body interaction tasks in unstructured environments. While recent advancements in Human-Object Interaction (HOI) have been substantial, prevailing methodologies predominantly address the manipulation of fully actuated objects, where the target is rigidly coupled to the robot's end-effector and its state is strictly constrained by the robot's kinematics. This paradigm neglects the pervasive class of underactuated objects characterized by independent dynamics and non-holonomic constraints, which pose significant control challenges due to complex coupling forces and frequent visual occlusions. To bridge this gap, we propose HAIC, a unified framework designed to enable robust interaction across a spectrum of object dynamics without reliance on external state estimation. Central to our approach is a novel dynamics predictor that infers high-order object states, specifically velocity and acceleration, solely from proprioceptive history. These predictions are explicitly projected onto static geometric priors to construct a spatially grounded representation of dynamic occupancy, allowing the policy to internalize collision boundaries and contact affordances in visual blind spots. We employ an asymmetric fine-tuning strategy where the world model continuously adapts to the student policyâs exploration, ensuring robust state estimation under distribution shifts. We evaluate our framework on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Empirical results demonstrate that HAIC achieves high success rates in agile object interactions, including skateboarding, cart pushing, and cart pulling under various weight load conditions, by proactively compensating for inertial physical perturbations, while HAIC simultaneously masters multi-object interaction involving long-horizon tasks and carrying a box across composed terrain by predicting the dynamics of multiple objects.
rss:2026-p013.authors: Dongting Li, Xingyu Chen, Qianyang Wu, Bo Chen, Sikai Wu, Hanyu Wu, Guoyao Zhang, Liang Li, Mingliang Zhou, Diyun Xiang, Jianzhu Ma, Qiang Zhang, Renjing Xu

rss:2026-p014.title: Collaborating Visual and Parameter Spaces for Consistent Long-Horizon Embodied World Model
rss:2026-p014.abstract: Embodied World Models (EWMs) have emerged as a scalable and risk-free paradigm for evaluating Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems. However, their reliability as evaluation benchmarks is often limited by the representation gap between low-dimensional actions and high-dimensional video synthesis. This gap leads to a lack of geometric correspondence, manifesting as accumulated trajectory drift and inconsistent object-robot interactions in long-horizon rollouts. To bridge this gap, we propose ViPSim, a framework that achieves consistent long-horizon generation through the synergistic collaboration of Visual and Parameter Spaces. We define the Visual Space as a domain of explicit spatial priors, integrating pixel-aligned projections of actions, camera perspectives, depth-informed scene geometry, and robot morphological masks to provide dense structural constraints. Concurrently, the Parameter Space is defined as a domain of numerical drivers that injects raw action sequences and camera matrices to provide precise motion guidance. By unifying these two spaces, ViPSim ensures that the generated states are simultaneously constrained by geometric boundaries and driven by precise numerical commands. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ViPSim is backbone-agnostic and significantly enhances trajectory consistency. Notably, our approach exhibits emergent capabilities in generating complex interactions with deformable objects (e.g., cloth folding) and maintains robust performance in out-of-distribution and cross-embodiment scenarios, providing a high-fidelity foundation for the automated evaluation of embodied intelligence.
rss:2026-p014.authors: Longyu Chen, Heng Li, Wei Yang, Manqi Zhao, Dongsheng Jiang

rss:2026-p015.title: Act2Goal: From World Model To General Goal-conditioned Policy
rss:2026-p015.abstract: Specifying robotic manipulation tasks in a manner that is both expressive and precise remains a central challenge. While visual goals provide a compact and unambiguous task specification, existing goal-conditioned policies often struggle with long-horizon manipulation due to their reliance on single-step action prediction without explicit modeling of task progress. We propose Act2Goal, a general goal-conditioned manipulation policy that integrates a goal-conditioned visual world model with multi-scale temporal control. Given a current observation and a target visual goal, the world model generates a plausible sequence of intermediate visual states that captures long-horizon structure. To translate this visual plan into robust execution, we introduce Multi-Scale Temporal Hashing, which decomposes the imagined trajectory into dense proximal frames for fine-grained closed-loop control and sparse distal frames that anchor global task consistency. The policy couples these representations with motor control through end-to-end cross-attention, enabling coherent long-horizon behavior while remaining reactive to local disturbances. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that Act2Goal, initialized from large-scale imitation learning, achieves strong performance across a wide range of long-horizon manipulation tasks. Beyond offline generalization, Act2Goal also supports reward-free online autonomous improvement via hindsight goal relabeling and LoRA-based finetuning, enabling rapid adaptation during deployment without external supervision. In real world experiments, it improves success rates from 30% to 90% on challenging out-of-distribution tasks within minutes of autonomous interaction, validating the effectiveness of online training as a powerful complement to offline learning.
rss:2026-p015.authors: Pengfei Zhou, Liliang Chen, Shengcong Chen, Di Chen, Wenzhi Zhao, Rongjun Jin, Guanghui Ren, Jianlan Luo

rss:2026-p016.title: Causal World Modeling for Robot Control
rss:2026-p016.abstract: This work highlights that video world modeling, alongside vision-language pre-training, establishes a distinct foundation for robot learning. By capturing environmental dynamics, video world models enable the robot to "imagine" near future statesâa capability essential for effective planning. Inspired by this, we introduce CauVA, an autoregressive diffusion framework that unifies frame prediction and action inference. Our approach features three key innovations: (1) an autoregressive Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) that processes visual frames and actions as a single causal sequence; (2) a history integration mechanism using KV cache to maintain temporal context from real-world interactions; and (3) a noisy latent augmentation strategy that enables decoding actions directly from intermediate denoised videos for fast inference. Evaluations on simulation and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that CauVA excels in complex manipulation, including long-horizon, high-precision, and deformable object tasks. Our code and models are publicly available.
rss:2026-p016.authors: Lin Li, Qihang Zhang, Yiming Luo, Shuai Yang, Ruilin Wang, Luyao Zhang, Mingrui Yu, Zelin Gao, Nan Xue, Boyu Zhou, Xing Zhu, Mingyu Ding, Yujun Shen, Yinghao Xu

rss:2026-p017.title: Simulation Distillation: Pretraining World Models in Simulation for Rapid Real-World Adaptation
rss:2026-p017.abstract: Simulation-to-real transfer remains a central challenge in robotics, as mismatches between simulated and real-world dynamics often lead to failures. While reinforcement learning offers a principled mechanism for adaptation, existing sim-to-real finetuning methods struggle with exploration and long-horizon credit assignment in the low-data regimes typical of real-world robotics. We introduce \texttt{Simulation Distillation} (\texttt{SimDist}), a sim-to-real framework that distills structural priors from a simulator into a latent world model and enables rapid real-world adaptation via online planning and supervised dynamics finetuning. By transferring reward and value models directly from simulation, \texttt{SimDist} provides dense planning signals from raw perception without requiring value learning during deployment. As a result, real-world adaptation reduces to short-horizon system identification, avoiding long-horizon credit assignment and enabling fast, stable improvement. Across precise manipulation and quadruped locomotion tasks, \texttt{SimDist} substantially outperforms prior methods in data efficiency, stability, and final performance.
rss:2026-p017.authors: Jacob Levy, Tyler Westenbroek, Kevin Huang, Fernando Palafox, Patrick Yin, Shayegan Omidshafiei, Dong-Ki Kim, Abhishek Gupta, David Fridovich-Keil

rss:2026-p018.title: Interactive World Simulator for Robot Policy Training and Evaluation
rss:2026-p018.abstract: Action-conditioned video prediction models (often referred to as world models) have shown strong potential for robotics applications, but existing world models are often slow and struggle to capture accurate physical interactions over long horizons, limiting their use for scalable robot policy training and evaluation. We present Interactive World Simulator, a framework that builds interactive world models using a moderate-sized robot interaction dataset and enables scalable robot policy training and evaluation. In our experiments, we show that our world models 1) produce physically accurate pixel-level predictions, and 2) support stable long-horizon interactions for more than 10 minutes at *15 FPS on a single RTX 4090 GPU*. Our framework uses data collected through interaction with the world models to train imitation policies, including Diffusion Policy, Action Chunking Transformer, and Ï-series policies. Through extensive real-world evaluation across diverse tasks involving rigid objects, deformable objects, object piles, and their interactions, we find that imitation policies trained on world-model-generated data perform comparably to policies trained on the same amount of real-world data. Additionally, we evaluate policies both within the world models and in the real world across diverse tasks, and observe a strong correlation between performance in the world models and in the real world. Together, these results establish the Interactive World Simulator as a stable and physically consistent surrogate that enables scalable robotic data generation and faithful, reproducible policy evaluation.
rss:2026-p018.authors: Yixuan Wang, Rhythm Syed, Fangyu Wu, Mengchao Zhang, Aykut Onol, Jose Barreiros, Hooshang Nayyeri, Tony Dear, Huan Zhang, Yunzhu Li

rss:2026-p021.title: Î¨â: An Open Foundation Model Towards Universal Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
rss:2026-p021.abstract: We introduce Î¨â (Psi-Zero), an open foundation model to address challenging humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. While existing approaches often attempt to address this fundamental problem by co-training on large and diverse human and humanoid data, we argue that this strategy is suboptimal due to the fundamental kinematic and motion disparities between humans and humanoid robots. Therefore, data efficiency and model performance remain unsatisfactory despite the considerable data volume. To address this challenge, Î¨â decouples the learning process to maximize the utility of heterogeneous data sources. Specifically, we propose a staged training paradigm with different learning objectives: First, we autoregressively pre-train a VLM backbone on large-scale egocentric human videos to acquire generalizable visual-action representations. Then, we post-train a flow-based action expert on high-quality humanoid robot data to learn precise robot joint control. Our research further identifies a critical yet often overlooked data recipe: in contrast to approaches that scale with noisy Internet clips or heterogeneous cross-embodiment robot datasets, we demonstrate that pre-training on high-quality egocentric human manipulation data followed by post-training on domain-specific real-world humanoid trajectories yields superior performance. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that \ours\ achieves the best performance using only about 800 hours of human video data and 30 hours of real-world robot data, outperforming baselines pre-trained on more than 10Ã as much data by over 40% in overall success rate across multiple real and simulation tasks. We will open-source the entire ecosystem to the community, including a data processing and training pipeline, a humanoid foundation model, and a real-time action inference engine.
rss:2026-p021.authors: Songlin Wei, Hongyi Jing, Boqian Li, Zhenyu Zhao, Jiageng Mao, Zhenhao Ni, Sicheng He, Sheng Zang, Xiawei Liu, Kaidi Kang, Jie Liu, Weiduo Yuan, Marco Pavone, Di Huang, Yue Wang

rss:2026-p023.title: Learning to Evolve: Multi-modal Interactive Fields for Robust Humanoid Navigation in Dynamic Environments
rss:2026-p023.abstract: Achieving safe manipulation-oriented navigation for humanoid robots is fundamentally challenged by two factors: locomotion-induced perceptual distortion (causing semantic-geometry distortion) and changes within the environment (causing map-reality mismatches). Existing static scene graphs often fail under these conditions, leading to interaction failures. To address this, we introduce the Multi-modal Interaction Field (MIF), a hierarchical framework that transforms the robot from a passive map-user into an active knowledge-evolver. MIF constructs three synergistic fields: (i) a denoised Appearance Field utilizing confidence-gated 3D Gaussian Splatting to suppress gait oscillation noise; (ii) a hierarchical Spatial Field for semantic reasoning; and (iii) Geometry Field, leveraging a Flow Matching based generative model to reconstruct high-fidelity meshes for rigorous Interaction Pose Safety (IPS) verification against the target object. Crucially, we propose a closed-loop Interaction and Adaptation Mechanism to adapt to environmental changes. By monitoring a multi-modal discrepancy score \mathcal{D}, the system autonomously distinguishes between sensor noise and genuine environmental changes (e.g., relocated objects), triggering a local evolution loop to rectify obsolete memory. Real-world experiments on a Unitree-G1 humanoid demonstrate that MIF significantly outperforms static baselines (HOV-SG), improving the success rate in dynamic relocation scenarios from 12% to 94%, while reducing semantic memory footprint by 91.4% via feature distillation.
rss:2026-p023.authors: Peifeng Jiang, Hong Liu, Jin Jin, Wenshuai Wang, Xia Li

rss:2026-p024.title: MOBIUS: A Multi-Modal Bipedal Robot that can Walk, Crawl, Climb, and Roll
rss:2026-p024.abstract: This paper presents the MOBIUS platform, a bipedal robot capable of walking, crawling, climbing, and rolling. MOBIUS features four limbs, two 6-DoF arms with two-finger grippers for manipulation and climbing, and two 4-DoF legs for locomotion--enabling smooth transitions across diverse terrains without reconfiguration. A hybrid control architecture combines reinforcement learning for locomotion and admittance control enhanced for safety by a Reference Governor and auto-tuning toward compliant contact interactions during manipulation. A high-level MIQCP planner autonomously selects locomotion modes to balance stability and energy efficiency. Hardware experiments demonstrate robust gait transitions, dynamic climbing, and full-body load support via pinch grasp. Overall, MOBIUS demonstrates the importance of tight integration between morphology, high-level planning, and control to enable mobile loco-manipulation and grasping, substantially expanding its interaction capabilities, workspace, and traversability.
rss:2026-p024.authors: Alexander Schperberg, Yusuke Tanaka, Stefano Di Cairano, Dennis Hong

rss:2026-p025.title: TeleGate: Whole-Body Humanoid Teleoperation via Gated Expert Selection with Motion Prior
rss:2026-p025.abstract: Real-time whole-body teleoperation is a critical method for humanoid robots to perform complex tasks in unstructured environments. However, developing a unified controller that robustly supports diverse human motions remains a significant challenge. Existing methods typically distill multiple expert policies into a single general policy, which often inevitably leads to performance degradation, particularly on highly dynamic motions. This paper presents TeleGate, a unified whole-body teleoperation framework for humanoid robots that achieves high-precision tracking across various motions while avoiding the performance loss inherent in knowledge distillation. Our key idea is to preserve the full capability of domain-specific expert policies by training a lightweight gating network, which dynamically activates experts in real-time based on proprioceptive states and reference trajectories. Furthermore, to compensate for the absence of future reference trajectories in real-time teleoperation, we introduce a VAE-based motion prior module that extracts implicit future motion intent from historical observations, enabling anticipatory control for motions requiring prediction such as jumping and standing up. We conducted empirical evaluations in simulation and also deployed our technique on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Using only 2.5 hours of motion capture data for training, our TeleGate achieves high-precision real-time teleoperation across diverse dynamic motions (e.g., running, fall recovery, and jumping), significantly outperforming the baseline methods in both tracking accuracy and success rate.
rss:2026-p025.authors: Jie Li, Bing Tang, Feng Wu

rss:2026-p027.title: Now You See That: Learning End-to-End Humanoid Locomotion from Raw Pixels
rss:2026-p027.abstract: Achieving robust vision-based humanoid locomotion remains challenging due to two fundamental issues: the sim-toreal gap introduces significant perception noise that degrades performance on fine-grained tasks, and training a unified policy across diverse terrains is hindered by conflicting learning objectives. To address these challenges, we present an end-to-end framework for vision-driven humanoid locomotion. For robust sim-to-real transfer, we develop a high-fidelity depth sensor simulation that captures stereo matching artifacts and calibration uncertainties inherent in real-world sensing. We further propose a vision-aware behavior distillation approach that combines latent space alignment with noise-invariant auxiliary tasks, enabling effective knowledge transfer from privileged height maps to noisy depth observations. For versatile terrain adaptation, we introduce terrain-specific reward shaping integrated with multi-critic and multi-discriminator learning, where dedicated networks capture the distinct dynamics and motion priors of each terrain type. We validate our approach on two humanoid platforms equipped with different stereo depth cameras. The resulting policy demonstrates robust performance across diverse environments, seamlessly handling extreme challenges such as high platforms and wide gaps, as well as fine-grained tasks including bidirectional long-term staircase traversal.
rss:2026-p027.authors: Wandong Sun, Yongbo Su, Guo Huang, Zilong Zhang, Wei Yingdong, Sen Xu, Sheng Cao, Xingwu Tian, Baoshi Cao, Yang Liu, Bin Yan, Yan Xie, Xie Zongwu

rss:2026-p028.title: Mind Your Steps: A General Learning Framework for Accurate Humanoid Foothold Tracking
