We present FTP-1, the first generalist foundation tactile policy pretrained to acquire transferable tactile manipulation abilities across diverse sensors and embodiments. FTP-1 supports varied tactile inputs, including image-, array-, and state-based signals, by using heterogeneous encoders to project them into unified morphology-aware latent tokens that are jointly modeled by a shared tactile Transformer expert. Pretrained on ~ 3,000 hours of tactile manipulation data aggregated from 26 data sources, spanning human and robot demonstrations across 21 sensors, FTP-1 learns tactile skills that transfer beyond the sensors seen during pretraining. Across downstream finetuning experiments spanning 5 hardware configurations, FTP-1 improves contact-rich manipulation on seen sensor setups by +17.2% and, surprisingly, transfers to two previously unseen tactile-sensor setups, achieving a +31% gain in success rate. FTP-1 establishes the first unified foundation baseline for tactile manipulation, providing future tactile policies with a shared model-level starting point. All model checkpoints, datasets, and training code will be released in the future.
openreview:xc8asDq7QI.authors: Chengbo Yuan, Zicheng Zhang, Mingjie Zhou, Wendi Chen, Yi Wang, Zhuoyang Liu, Dantong Niu, Shuo Wang, Hui Zhang, Wenkang Zhang, Yingdong Hu, Yuanqing Gong, Wanli Xing, Chuan Wen, Cewu Lu, Kaifeng Zhang, Yang Gao

openreview:xaGVjPTxtr.title: VISTA: Vision-Grounded and Physics-Validated Adaptation of UMI data for VLA Training
openreview:xaGVjPTxtr.abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enables scalable data collection without target-robot teleoperation, but UMI-style demonstrations are not directly suited for large-scale Vision-Language-Action (VLA) training. We identify the challenge of training VLA models from UMI-collected data as a dual adaptation problem: (i) wrist-mounted fisheye observations are misaligned with the visual distributions of pretrained vision-language models, and (ii) human-collected trajectories are not guaranteed to be executable under target-robot embodiment constraints. To mitigate this challenge, we present VISTA, a framework that adapts UMI-collected data to VLA training through fisheye-aligned visual grounding and embodiment-conditioned trajectory validation. UMI-VQA supplies vision-language supervision under wrist-mounted fisheye observations, while trajectory validation scores human-collected demonstrations by continuity, self-collision risk, and execution fidelity to select physically plausible action supervision before training. VISTA then uses the adapted visual-language data and validated trajectories in a two-stage VLA training procedure. Experiments show that UMI-VQA improves policy performance over action-only training and standard-view VQA, while validation scores are predictive of real-robot deployment success. Across UMI-style simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, VISTA consistently improves over strong VLA baselines including $\pi_{0.5}$, LingBot-VLA, and Wall-X. We will release the pipeline, datasets, and pretrained model.
openreview:xaGVjPTxtr.authors: Siyuan Yang, Linzheng Guo, ouyang lu, Zhaxizhuoma, Zhang Daoran, Xinmiao Wang, Ting Xiao, Fangzheng YAN, Zhijun Chen, Yan Ding, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li

openreview:xXHKqL5u5P.title: Active Generative Simulation: Meta-Learning What to Simulate for Sim-and-Real Policy Co-Training
openreview:xXHKqL5u5P.abstract: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate Active Generative Simulation: optimizing a simulator's data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility simulation parameter distributions without human heuristics. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable.
openreview:xXHKqL5u5P.authors: Liqian Ma, Vaibhav Saxena, Utkarsh Aashu Mishra, Shuo Cheng, Yongxin Chen, Danfei Xu

openreview:xWoyO2BPcl.title: RoboAffect: Egocentric Emotion Reasoning for Robot Companions in Shared Viewing
openreview:xWoyO2BPcl.abstract: Robot learning has made rapid progress in control, manipulation, and navigation, yet the affective capabilities of companion robots remain largely unexplored. Watching movies together with humans provides a natural and emotionally rich setting for studying robot affective perception and response. It requires robots to understand viewer-level emotion and remain robust to first-person-view (FPV) screen observations. In RoboAffect, we introduce EgoScreen-Emotion (ESE), the first benchmark dataset for robot affective perception from shared viewing. ESE contains 224 movie trailers and 28,667 egocentric keyframes captured under 18 systematic viewing conditions (camera height, viewing distance, and horizontal angle), annotated by 5 raters with multi-label confidence scores. Inter-annotator agreement reaches Fleiss’ κ=0.34 overall and κ=0.72 on high-confidence frames. We demonstrate a significant FPV domain gap: Macro-F1 drops from 28.06 to 14.64 under Raw→FPV transfer, corresponding to a 47.8% relative decline, motivating FPV-matched training for reliable affective perception on robots. Building on ESE, we develop a multimodal long-context framework integrating 3-frame visuals, synchronized audio, and narrative summaries, trained with confidence-aware aggregation and label smoothing to handle affective ambiguity. Our full model achieves Macro-F1 32.74, reaching 84.3% of the human leave-one-out reference (38.82) and outperforming all zero-shot baselines including Gemini-2.5-Flash (23.50). We further validate the pipeline on a physical quadruped robot, demonstrating end-to-end affective perception and expression under real FPV conditions. Dataset, code, and model weights will be released for reproducibility.
openreview:xWoyO2BPcl.authors: Ze Dong, Hao Shi, Zejia GAO, Zhonghua Yi, Kaiwei Wang, Lin Wang

openreview:xOhVCWilYJ.title: More than a Point: Adaptive Affordance Heatmaps as VLM Grounding Interfaces for Robotics
openreview:xOhVCWilYJ.abstract: Hierarchical VLM-based robotic systems often use sparse points or bounding boxes as intermediate spatial representations, which are inadequate for region-level grounding. This is particularly evident in instructions such as place near the bowl, which specify a feasible region rather than a single target point. We present RoboMAP, a VLM-based robotic grounding framework that uses adaptive affordance heatmaps as a language-conditioned intermediate interface between spatial reasoning and downstream modules. RoboMAP predicts dense score maps for continuous and object-free target regions, exposing feasible spatial support that downstream segmentation, grasping, and control modules can use beyond sparse prompts alone. To enable scalable training without manual dense labels, RoboMAP synthesizes heatmap supervision from heterogeneous annotations, including points, boxes, and robot trajectory data. Across four spatial grounding benchmarks evaluated with standard point-extraction metrics, RoboMAP obtains the best reported accuracy on three benchmarks while maintaining a 0.04 s grounding-stage forward pass. In 50 real-world dual-arm manipulation trials spanning five tabletop task types, it achieves an 82% success rate using heatmap-guided segmentation and grasp proposal. We further provide qualitative cross-embodiment demonstrations across manipulation and navigation scenarios.
openreview:xOhVCWilYJ.authors: Xinyu Shao, TANG YANZHE, Pengwei Xie, Long ZENG, Xiu Li

openreview:xMysKLF2hX.title: RoboFQE: Rollout-Free Evaluation of Visual Robot Policies from Offline Trajectories
openreview:xMysKLF2hX.abstract: Evaluating robot policies before deployment typically requires producing new trajectories through real-world execution, simulators, or learned world models. These rollout-based approaches impose infrastructure requirements; simulator and world-model evaluators additionally face prediction errors that can compound over the evaluation horizon. In this paper, we study off-policy evaluation as an alternative to rollout-based robot-policy evaluation methods. Specifically, we introduce RoboFQE, an evaluator that estimates the discounted expected return of a target policy from offline robot trajectories without estimating a behavior-policy density, combining fitted Q-evaluation with a pretrained vision foundation model and learned terminal success annotation to bridge the gap between standard OPE benchmarks and continuous-control visual manipulation. Controlled experiments across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that RoboFQE produces accurate discounted-return estimates and preserves policy rankings even on long-horizon manipulation tasks where video world-model evaluators are degraded by autoregressive prediction errors. Ablation experiments show that pretrained vision encoders substantially outperform from-scratch alternatives, particularly on long-horizon tasks, and that learned terminal success annotation enables evaluation without ground-truth reward labels with only slight reduction of accuracy.
openreview:xMysKLF2hX.authors: Yunfu Deng, Sangwoo Shin, Brahma S Pavse, Josiah P. Hanna

openreview:xL2eR7x00h.title: Discovering Control Symmetries via Transition Manifold Tangency
openreview:xL2eR7x00h.abstract: Equivariant architectures improve sample efficiency and generalization in robot learning, but they require the symmetry group to be specified in advance. Existing symmetry-discovery methods focus on static datasets, autonomous dynamical systems, or input--output mappings without separate action representations, and to our knowledge none directly addresses controlled transition datasets $\{(s_i,a_i,s_i')\}$, where actions transform under their own representation and data distribution introduced by the behaviour policy need not be symmetric. We introduce \emph{Transition-Manifold Tangency} (TMT), a geometric framework for discovering symmetries from transition data. Valid transitions form a submanifold of state--action--next-state space, and a dynamical symmetry must move along it: every infinitesimal generator is tangent to this manifold. The estimation target -- the local normal frame -- depends on data geometry but not on the density along the manifold, which yields robustness to nonlinear dynamics and to asymmetric behaviour policies. We provide a model-free local-PCA estimator (TMT-KNN) and a denoiser-based estimator (TMT-NN), and extend both to discrete symmetry discovery via a manifold-consistency test. On continuous benchmarks TMT-NN recovers the ground-truth generator subspace where Jacobian-based and distribution-matching baselines fail under nonlinear dynamics and policy bias respectively. On discrete benchmarks, TMT-NN's candidates approach the denoiser noise floor in absolute manifold distance while a ratio-based metric favours the near-identity candidates of distribution-matching baselines.

openreview:xHjEeyHkhY.title: ORD-WM: Learning Object-Centric Rigid Dynamics for 3D World Modeling in Robotic Manipulation
openreview:xHjEeyHkhY.abstract: World models provide robots with a predictive mechanism for reasoning about how actions change object states in manipulation tasks. However, existing image-based and dense 3D world models do not explicitly impose object-level rigid motion, leaving rigid-object geometry preservation to be learned implicitly and making multi-step rollouts susceptible to shape drift or object-level motion inconsistency. To address this, we propose ORD-WM, a 3D world model that learns object-centric rigid dynamics for robotic manipulation. ORD-WM learns a vector-neuron variational autoencoder supervised by signed distance fields, which encodes each object point cloud as a geometry-aware latent representation composed of 3D vector features, and uses an action-conditioned dynamics model to predict object-wise SE(3) motion increments. Rather than generating unconstrained next latent states, ORD-WM analytically applies predicted object-wise rigid transformations to the current latent states, separating persistent object geometry from pose changes. Experiments show that ORD-WM enables stable, geometry-preserving multi-step prediction and supports efficient real-time replanning for closed-loop model predictive control in simulated and real-world manipulation scenarios. More details and videos are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/ORD-WM.
openreview:xHjEeyHkhY.authors: Yueyang Weng, Xiaopeng Zhang, Yuxi Ou, Mu Yongjin, Chengzhi zhao, Yanjie Li

openreview:xEOer7gykg.title: Gaze Prompts: Temporally Dense Human Attention for Vision–Language–Action Fine-Tuning
openreview:xEOer7gykg.abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) fine-tuning supplies dense per-frame visual--action supervision but leaves implicit which part of the scene the demonstrator treated as task-relevant at each timestep---what we call the instruction's \emph{temporal grounding}. We introduce \emph{eye-tracker-supervised gaze prompting} to supply this signal: an HMD eye tracker records the operator's fixation during VR teleoperation, a lightweight predictor (${\sim}50$M parameters) learns to estimate fixation from RGB and language, and the prediction is rendered as a crosshair on the image input of an unchanged $\pi_0$ policy---with no eye tracker or architectural modification at deployment. Across six real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, gaze prompting improves over standard fine-tuning on every task, raising mean success rate from $26.3\%$ to $56.0\%$. Two isolations explain the gains: (i)~with the gaze signal fixed, the input-pixel route carries two signatures of temporal grounding to the policy---instruction-conditional attention and per-frame stage awareness over long horizons---that an auxiliary attention loss on the same gaze does not; and (ii)~under the same route, real human gaze outperforms detection and random cues, with the gap explained by a third signature, anticipation, that engineered cues structurally cannot supply.
openreview:xEOer7gykg.authors: Yihan Zhou, Rui Yan, Mingcong Li, Zheyuan Huang, Xu Yang, Guo Xueyang, Yilin Mo

openreview:x05Rf7L7H4.title: Where Small Mistakes Matter: Quantifying State Criticality for Imitation Learning
openreview:x05Rf7L7H4.abstract: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success.
openreview:x05Rf7L7H4.authors: Yusuf Umut Ciftci, Joonwon Kang, Ajay Suresha Sathya, Somil Bansal

openreview:wiovp2zRWA.title: Current as Touch: Proprioceptive Contact Feedback for Compliant Dexterous Manipulation
openreview:wiovp2zRWA.abstract: Compliance is essential for dexterous manipulation, yet existing solutions often rely on external tactile or force sensors that are costly, fragile, and difficult to deploy on low-cost robot hands. We propose a proprioception-driven framework that learns tactile-like contact feedback from motor current and joint states. Since motor current is closely related to actuator torque, it provides an intrinsic signal for perceiving contact force, object resistance, and grasp stability without additional sensing hardware. Rather than estimating external wrenches or commanding torque, our method predicts a compliance reference position: an ideal joint-position target for a standard PD controller whose induced position error generates appropriate grasping force. This position-based formulation is compatible with mainstream teleoperation and policy-learning pipelines, while enabling the robot to adapt interaction forces from real-time proprioceptive feedback. Thus, motor current serves not only as a force proxy but also as a learnable proprioceptive contact signal for compliance reference prediction. Experiments on multiple dexterous hands and contact-rich tasks, including fragile object handling, dynamic load adaptation, sustained surface contact, and thin-object retrieval, show stable compliant grasping, safer and more efficient teleoperation, and improved downstream policy learning without external tactile sensors.
openreview:wiovp2zRWA.authors: Chenyang Ma, Yunchao Yao, Zhenyu Wei, Ruogu Li, Daniel Szafir, Mingyu Ding

openreview:wXv81vB0Xt.title: ELASTIC: Efficiently Learning to Adaptively Scale Test-Time Compute for Generative Control Policies
openreview:wXv81vB0Xt.abstract: Generative control policies (GCPs), such as diffusion policies and flow-based vision-language-action models, enable test-time scaling in robot control. This compute can be allocated along two axes: *sequential scaling*, which increases denoising steps to refine actions, and *parallel scaling*, which samples multiple candidate actions to search across modes of the policy distribution. Existing methods typically rely on fixed conservative schedules that may over-compute in easy states and under-allocate in difficult ones. However, the optimal allocation is hard to know a priori as it is state-, task-, and policy-dependent: early stages of a grasp may benefit from broader parallel exploration, while near-contact phases may require more sequential refinement for precision. We present ELASTIC, an algorithm that learns state-dependent test-time compute schedules for GCPs. We formulate compute allocation as a meta-Markov Decision Process in which a meta-policy interacts with a frozen pretrained robot policy and selects sequential steps and parallel samples at each denoising iteration to maximize task success while minimizing compute. Using reinforcement learning, this meta-policy also learns adaptive compute schedules without access to the GCP's training data. Across simulated manipulation benchmarks with diffusion policies, ELASTIC Pareto-dominates fixed and single-axis scaling baselines at matched compute budgets. On real-world robot manipulation with the $\pi_{0.5}$ vision-language-action model, ELASTIC matches best-of-$10$ success while reducing wall-clock latency by 34%.
openreview:wXv81vB0Xt.authors: Andrew Zou Li, Gokul Swamy, Yonatan Bisk, Andrea Bajcsy

openreview:wRLEgpRnVR.title: ActionCodec: What Makes for Good Action Tokenizers
openreview:wRLEgpRnVR.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models leveraging the native autoregressive paradigm of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated superior instruction-following and training efficiency. Central to this paradigm is action tokenization, yet its design has primarily focused on reconstruction fidelity, failing to address its direct impact on VLA optimization. Consequently, the fundamental question of what makes for good action tokenizers remains unanswered. In this paper, we bridge this gap by establishing design principles specifically from the perspective of VLA optimization. We identify a set of best practices based on information-theoretic insights, including maximized temporal token overlap, minimized vocabulary redundancy, enhanced multimodal mutual information and token independence. Guided by these principles, we introduce ActionCodec, a high-performance action tokenizer that significantly enhances both training efficiency and VLA performance across diverse simulation and real-world benchmarks. Notably, on LIBERO, a SmolVLM2-2.2B fine-tuned with ActionCodec achieves a 95.5% success rate without any robotics pre-training. With advanced architectural enhancements, this reaches 97.4%, representing a new SOTA for VLA models without robotics pre-training. We believe our established design principles, alongside the released model, will provide a clear roadmap for the community to develop more effective action tokenizers. Code and checkpoints are available at https://anonymous.link.
openreview:wRLEgpRnVR.authors: Zibin Dong, Yicheng Liu, Shiduo Zhang, Baijun Ye, Yifu Yuan, Fei Ni, Jingjing Gong, Xipeng Qiu, Hang Zhao, Yinchuan Li, Jianye HAO

openreview:wMrKZ9eYBg.title: LAPT-Scale: Scaling Embodied Policies with Latent Action Pre-Training on Human Videos
openreview:wMrKZ9eYBg.abstract: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours.
openreview:wMrKZ9eYBg.authors: Zhiyuan Xiang, Peidong Liu, Mingyang Li, Jiawei Li, Wenhow Li, Wenbo Ding, Xiang Deng

openreview:wLgEYxjqid.title: OPENDEXGRASP: Open-vocabulary Task-Oriented Dexterous Grasping
openreview:wLgEYxjqid.abstract: Robust dexterous grasp synthesis has made substantial progress in generating stable, diverse, and physically plausible hand poses. Yet grasping in real manipulation is rarely task-agnostic: a functional grasp must preserve the action possibility specified by the task, contact the appropriate object region, and remain executable by a high-DoF hand. We study open-vocabulary task-oriented dexterous grasp pose generation, where a robot observes multi-view visual inputs, 3D object geometry, and a free-form language instruction, and must generate a grasp that is both physically feasible and functionally aligned. The central challenge is to establish a generalizable perception-action mapping across open-ended task semantics, functional contact selection, and dexterous hand pose generation. We present O PEN D EX G RASP, a unified data, training, and generative modeling framework. At the data level, we build OpenDexVerse, a dualsource data ecosystem constructed by a C2A Recipe (Coverage-to-Alignment): OpenDex-Scale provides broad open-vocabulary coverage through large-scale optimization-generated grasps with vision-language semantic annotation, while OpenDex-Align supplies high-quality embodied functional alignment through human teleoperation and category-level transfer. At the model level, O PEN D EX G RASP learns a shared semantic-geometric latent space that couples multi-view language-conditioned perception with 3D geometric structure. Affordance prediction and grasp pose generation are treated as complementary supervision views over this latent space, allowing the model to ground functional regions while directly generating task-consistent dexterous grasps. Extensive simulation and realrobot experiments show that O PEN D EX G RASP improves open-vocabulary task generalization, functional-region alignment, physical feasibility, inference efficiency, and real-world execution success.
openreview:wLgEYxjqid.authors: Jiyao Zhang, Junhan Wang, Tianyu Wang, Zeyuan Chen, Anthony Bolton, Yitong Peng, Hao Dong

openreview:wKRawikMuG.title: Modular Sensory Stream for Integrating Physical Feedback in Vision-Language-Action Models
openreview:wKRawikMuG.abstract: Humans understand and interact with the real world by relying on diverse physical feedback beyond visual perception. Motivated by this, recent approaches attempt to incorporate physical sensory signals into Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs). However, they typically focus on a single type of physical signal, failing to capture the heterogeneous and complementary nature of real-world interactions. In this paper, we propose MoSS, a modular sensory stream framework that adapts VLAs to leverage multiple sensory signals for action prediction. Specifically, we introduce decoupled modality streams that integrate heterogeneous physical signals into the action stream via joint cross-modal self-attention. To enable stable incorporation of new modalities, we adopt a two-stage training scheme that freezes pretrained VLA parameters in the early stage. Furthermore, to better capture contact interaction dynamics, we incorporate an auxiliary task that predicts future physical signals. Through extensive real-world experiments, we demonstrate that MoSS successfully augments VLAs to leverage diverse physical signals (i.e., tactile, force, and torque), integrating multiple signals to achieve synergistic performance gains. The $\text{\href{https:\//corl-moss.github.io/}{project page}}$ is available.
openreview:wKRawikMuG.authors: Jimin Lee, Huiwon Jang, Myungkyu Koo, Jungwoo Park, Jinwoo Shin

openreview:wALhOwQWnx.title: Learning Functional Compliance in Whole-body Manipulation
openreview:wALhOwQWnx.abstract: Compliant whole-body controllers for humanoids achieve safety by uniformly relaxing stiffness across all directions, but this dissolves the control authority needed for contact-rich tasks, forcing a hard trade-off between safety and performance. We introduce \textit{functional compliance}: a task-dependent compliant control scheme that preserves authority along task-relevant axes while staying compliant elsewhere, varying in both direction and time. We simultaneously learn a control policy using a reward shaped by compliant poses and a force estimator that can be used at deploy time to compose variable compliance profiles. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three contact-rich whole-body manipulation tasks on the Unitree G1. Our method matches state-of-the-art motion-tracking fidelity while improving task success on key insertion and book reorientation, where directional and time-varying compliance is required, and matching the strongest baseline on cabinet opening, where it is not. This suggests that task-specific variable compliance, not constant uniform relaxation, is the correct whole-body control primitive for humanoid manipulation.
openreview:wALhOwQWnx.authors: Gio Huh, Yue Zhuo, Zehua Wang, Alan Yu, Yibo Cheng, Yanbing Han, Gabriel B. Margolis, Ge Yang

openreview:w3g5PWur7i.title: MobiAgent: Dual-Loop Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
openreview:w3g5PWur7i.abstract: Long-horizon mobile manipulation presents significant challenges due to compounding execution errors and capacity interference between locomotion and arm control. While recent Vision-Language-Action models excel at short-horizon tasks, they lack the hierarchical reasoning required for multi-stage objectives. Furthermore, existing hierarchical agents suffer from rigid sub-task mapping, inflexible replanning, and a lack of continuous learning. To address these limitations, we introduce MobiAgent, a dual-loop agentic framework that bridges robust deployment execution and continuous policy evolution. During deployment, the Inner Loop decouples high-level reasoning from low-level control through highly composable \textit{atomic skills}. It employs Vision-Language models for receding-horizon planning and visual reflection, dynamically composing skills to ensure robust error recovery. These skills are executed by specialized flow-matching experts that share a unified VLM backbone, maximizing reusability while mitigating capacity interference. Concurrently, the Outer Loop drives automated lifelong learning by autonomously segmenting and verifying deployment rollouts, clustering them to discover atomic skills, and continuously fine-tuning the skill library without human annotations. Evaluations across the simulated BEHAVIOR-1K benchmark and real-world tasks demonstrate that MobiAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art monolithic VLAs, achieving a +22.5% higher success rate in simulation. Furthermore, it demonstrates robust error recovery against critical failures and enables steady, annotation-free policy evolution via autonomous data recycling.
openreview:w3g5PWur7i.authors: Chenzhi Liu, Yue Zhang, Jiehong Lin, Jianan Wang, Bo Wang, Zhongrui Wang, Xiaojuan Qi

openreview:w2H90oEzfp.title: ForceBand: Learning Forceful Manipulation with sEMG
openreview:w2H90oEzfp.abstract: Human demonstrations are a scalable data source for learning robot manipulation policies. However, common human demonstrations, such as motion-capture trajectories and internet videos, do not capture the contact forces that are critical for forceful manipulation. In this paper, we introduce ForceBand a low-cost wrist-worn sEMG system for turning human muscle activity into force-enriched demonstrations. We first collect a 10-hour multimodal dataset containing egocentric video, sEMG, IMU, and fingertip forces across diverse actions and objects.  Using this dataset, we train an EMG2Force model that predicts per-finger forces from sEMG and IMU signals after a short user-specific calibration. After calibration, users can collect target-task demonstrations using only the wristband and video; EMG2Force then labels these demonstrations with per-finger force traces, producing force-augmented demonstrations for robot policy learning. Experiments show that ForceBand recovers fine-grained fingertip interactions with over 50% lower force prediction error than vision-based baselines, and achieves an 87% success rate on pick, squeeze, and place tasks that require object specific force control across objects with diverse shapes, sizes, and weights.
openreview:w2H90oEzfp.authors: Botao He, Zhi Wang, Linna Kuang, Ishaan Ghosh, Jitendra Malik, Cornelia Fermuller, Tingfan Wu, Jiayuan Mao, Ruoshi Liu, Haozhi Qi, Yiannis Aloimonos

openreview:w1x9MHo93E.title: Worlds in One Demo: A Synthetic Data Engine for Learning Open-World Mobile Manipulation
openreview:w1x9MHo93E.abstract: Learning open-world mobile manipulation policies requires vast data to achieve spatial generalization, long-horizon robustness, and scene generalization. Current prevailing data collection paradigms, teleoperation and UMI, would require dramatic human effort and cost at scale. We introduce WANDA: learning open-World mobile mANipulation from one demonstration via a synthetic DAta engine. WANDA first reconstructs background Gaussian splats and robot-object interaction trajectories from source RGBD observations, as a world substrate for later planning and rendering. It then rearranges contact-rich robot-object interaction segments into extensive spatial configurations, utilizing whole-body motion planning to chain them into new trajectories. To enhance long-horizon robustness, it applies Corrective State Expansion to increase the robot and object state diversity at different stages of mobile manipulation trajectories. To unlock scene generalization, novel trajectories are synthesized on generated 3D worlds from daily captured photos. We then combine Gaussian splatting for backgrounds and Isaac Sim rendering for reconstructed objects to render photo-realistic visual observations. We evaluate our data generation pipeline on extensive simulation and real-world tasks across environments. The policies trained from our synthetic data engine achieve strong spatial and scene generalization from one real demonstration.
openreview:w1x9MHo93E.authors: Lingxiao Guo, Huanyu Li, Guanya Shi

openreview:vQmF2cR04D.title: HuRo: Robotizing Human Videos for Scalable VLA Pretraining
openreview:vQmF2cR04D.abstract: Human video datasets have emerged as a compelling way to alternative to expensive real-robot data, leveraging visual diversity present in human videos. To bridge the inherent human-to-robot embodiment gap, existing methods either constrain video sources to narrow, task-aligned environments or focus solely on visual representation transfer while leaving the underlying action trajectories unutilized. In this work, we focus on robotized video as a means to further capitalize on human data, examining its effectiveness as a scalable source for policy pretraining.   To this end, we propose a robotization pipeline capable of handling heterogeneous human videos, effectively accommodating different levels of initial annotation by inferring missing intermediate signals.   Building on this pipeline, we construct the HuRo Dataset, a large scale collection containing about 630K robotized episodes and 142M processed frames converted from a wide variety of human video sources.   Across four real-world downstream manipulation tasks, we show performance scales with the amount of robotized pretraining data. Policies pretrained on our dataset surpass strong baseline foundation models that were pretrained solely on large scale, purely robotic data. These results suggest that robotized human videos can serve as a practical and scalable source of supervision for robot policy learning.
openreview:vQmF2cR04D.authors: Jinho Jeong, Se June Joo, Jaehyun Kang, Dongyun Kim, Yena Kim, Hanjung Kim, Seon Joo Kim

openreview:vG6UymddY4.title: OmniTacTune: Policy-Agnostic Real-World RL for Tactile Residual Adaptation of Visual Policies
openreview:vG6UymddY4.abstract: Visual policies learned from human videos, teleoperation, and robot demonstrations offer scalable motion priors, but often fail in contact-rich manipulation, where success significantly depends on local force and contact geometry. Tactile sensing provides these complementary signals, yet tactile data remain costly to collect and hard to generalize across sensors, robots, and tasks. We introduce OmniTacTune, a policy-agnostic real-world RL pipeline that adapts tactile feedback to pretrained visual policies through residual correction. OmniTacTune uses a two-stage design: it first warm-starts tactile-aware learning from autonomous base-policy rollouts, then learns a lightweight tactile residual policy through online interaction. Extensive experiments show that OmniTacTune generalizes across diverse contact-rich tasks, visual base policies, and tactile representations. Across four real-world contact-rich tasks, it improves visual base policies from 5–40% success to 85–100% within 40–80 minutes, demonstrating an efficient path for adapting tactile feedback to scalable visual robot policies.
openreview:vG6UymddY4.authors: Kelin Yu, Haode Zhang, Harish Ravichandar, Yunhai Han, Ruohan Gao

openreview:v24DO7JOuN.title: MoRE: Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Physics Robotic World Models
openreview:v24DO7JOuN.abstract: A robotic world model should predict how objects evolve under robot actions and physical dynamics. While recent 3D world modeling approaches have made progress toward general robotic prediction, they often struggle to capture the heterogeneous dynamics underlying diverse object interactions. In this paper, we propose MoRE, a novel 3D world model that organizes robotic dynamics into rigid, deformable, and prehensile regimes using a mixture of motion experts built on a shared encoder backbone. This design enables a single model to capture diverse physical behaviors while preserving regime-specific inductive biases. We train a 1B-parameter version of MoRE on a mixture of simulation data generated in Isaac Sim and real-world robotic interaction data. We further integrate MoRE with Model Predictive Control (MPC), enabling a range of manipulation tasks with a unified model. Experiments show that MoRE consistently improves prediction accuracy across rigid, deformable, and prehensile interaction benchmarks, leading to stronger real-world MPC performance.
openreview:v24DO7JOuN.authors: Ziyu Zhu, Shaowei Liu, Albert J. Zhai, Henry Che, Wei-Chiu Ma, Shenlong Wang

openreview:ult1vxdeUb.title: Visible Touch: Rendering Contact for Visuomotor Policies
openreview:ult1vxdeUb.abstract: Integrating contact information into visuomotor policies remains an open problem. Touch is essential to robust manipulation, yet most modern policies, including pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models, operate from vision and proprioception alone. Existing approaches to closing this gap require specialized tactile hardware, add separate tactile encoders, or commit to non-image policy backbones, all incompatible with the modern paradigm of image-conditioned policies built on pretrained 2D visual representations. Our key insight is that the bottleneck is not the contact information itself, but how it is delivered: when contact signals are exposed in the same spatial frame as the scene the policy already attends to, they become directly usable by any image-conditioned policy without architectural changes. We operationalize this insight in Visible Touch, paired with a custom low-cost magnetic contact sensor that is open-sourced and fabricated from off-the-shelf parts via a parametric CAD-to-mold pipeline. Across the LIBERO benchmark, Visible Touch improves BC-Transformer success rates by 16 percentage points on average, with controlled comparisons showing that how contact is represented matters more than what contact information is provided. The pattern holds when fine-tuning pretrained VLAs: miniVLA on LIBERO gains 29 points on average, and $\pi_{0.5}$ on four real-world contact-rich tasks gains 30 points with our custom sensor.
openreview:ult1vxdeUb.authors: Metin Alp Dogan, Edward Sun, Feng Xu, Daniel Wu, Allen Peng, Dennis Hong, Yuchen Cui

openreview:uizBY3yrgz.title: RoboGene: Diversity-Driven Agentic Task Generation Framework for VLA Pre-training
openreview:uizBY3yrgz.abstract: The pursuit of general-purpose robotic manipulation is hindered by the scarcity of diverse, real-world interaction data. Unlike the large-scale web vision-language data, robotic data collection is an active process incurring prohibitive physical costs. As a result, the key challenge is not merely to collect more robot data, but to obtain training data that provides informative learning knowledge by broadening behavioral coverage and capturing meaningful variations in objects, scenes, and skills. However, how to automatically curate task proposals that maximize the utility of collected robot data remains a critical yet under-explored challenge.  To address this, we introduce RoboGene, an agentic framework designed to automate the generation of diverse and informative manipulation tasks across heterogeneous robotic embodiments, spanning single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile robots. RoboGene integrates three core components: (1) diversity-driven sampling for broad task coverage, (2) agentic self-reflection for task-quality assessment, and (3) human-verified feedback memory for execution-grounded validation and continual refinement. We conduct extensive quantitative analysis and large-scale real-world experiments, collecting datasets of 18k trajectories and introducing novel metrics to assess task quality in terms of feasibility and diversity. Results demonstrate that RoboGene significantly outperforms frontier foundation models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro). Furthermore, real-world experiments show that VLA models trained on data generated by RoboGene achieve higher success rates and stronger generalization, highlighting the importance of high-quality task generation. Our project is available at https://x-robogene.github.io/.
openreview:uizBY3yrgz.authors: Yixue Zhang, Kun Wu, Zhi Gao, Zhen Zhao, Pei Ren, Zhiyuan Xu, Fei Liao, Xinhua Wang, Shichao Fan, Di Wu, Qiuxuan Feng, Meng Li, Zhengping Che, Chang Liu, Jian Tang

openreview:uhnmcdamCa.title: NAC: Neural Action Codec for Vision-Language-Action Models
openreview:uhnmcdamCa.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models rely on discrete action tokenizers to bridge continuous robot control and autoregressive sequence modeling, yet existing tokenizers often trade off between compression, latency, and downstream performance. We revisit this design through the lens of neural audio codecs—convolutional encoder–decoder architectures with residual vector quantization that serve as the standard front end for audio foundation models. Motivated by their success, we introduce the Neural Action Codec (NAC), which treats short robot action trajectories as multi-channel 1D signals and compresses them using a multi-scale RVQGAN architecture. We observe that audio-specific mel-spectrogram objectives are ill-suited for kinematic signals; however, by replacing them with simple time-domain and non-mel spectral reconstruction losses, audio-codec-style models can autoencode actions with high fidelity without substantial architectural changes. NAC provides a compact, ordered token space via offset codebooks, enabling standard autoregressive policies to operate over short, structured sequences. Meanwhile, a Vocos-style decoder with an ISTFT head and adversarial discriminators recovers smooth, detailed trajectories. Across LIBERO-10, RoboMimic, and a suite of real-world manipulation tasks, NAC achieves lower reconstruction error and higher success rates than binning, FAST, and prior VQ-based tokenizers at comparable or better compression rates. These results demonstrate that repurposed neural audio codecs offer a strong, practical backbone for learned action tokenization in modern VLAs.

openreview:uZalcCyrVl.title: Counterfactual Video Generation Enables Scalable Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
openreview:uZalcCyrVl.abstract: Teaching humanoids loco-manipulation skills, such as carrying diverse objects, via visual imitation is a promising path toward generalist robots. However, acquiring high-quality, full-body human videos that span a wide variety of object interactions is difficult, leaving too few demonstrations to learn a generalist policy. We propose PRISM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that overcomes this limitation by amplifying a handful of real videos into a large, diverse training set. PRISM first generates hundreds of diverse ``counterfactual'' human–object interaction videos via video-to-video (V2V) generation from a few exemplar real videos. Our contact-anchored real-to-sim pipeline then reconstructs both human and object motions, retargeting this imperfect video data into physically plausible trajectories. The intra-class variability across these counterfactual videos lets us train a single policy that generalizes to unseen objects within each category. We demonstrate the full pipeline by deploying this policy on a real robot without any real-world fine-tuning. Using only onboard depth observations, our humanoid picks up, carries, and drops objects—including boxes, barrels, bins, and balls---across novel instances, sizes, and initial configurations.
openreview:uZalcCyrVl.authors: Zihan Wang, Zhen Wu, Pieter Abbeel, Rocky Duan, Jitendra Malik, Carmelo Sferrazza, Karen Liu, Guanya Shi, Angjoo Kanazawa

openreview:uNi5VigrGr.title: Optimal Transport Q-Learning for Flow Policy Steering and Acceleration
openreview:uNi5VigrGr.abstract: Diffusion and flow policies have recently demonstrated remarkable performance in robotic applications by accurately capturing multimodal robot trajectory distributions, especially in the context of vision language action (VLA) models. However, high quality policy performance also requires fast inference and high quality demonstrations, which are often hard to get. Lack of these leads to suboptimal policy behaviors and failure under distribution shifts. In this work we address the problem of fine-tuning and accelerating suboptimal flow-based policies using the robot's experience through RL post-training. We introduce Optimal Transport Q-Learning (OTQL), a new methodology for finetuning flow policies using advantage weighted conditional optimal transport flow matching. OTQL can finetune and accelerate flows with an interaction budget of 50-60 episodes while avoiding computationally expensive distillation in simulation and real-world robot tasks. Our results show that OTQL post-trains flow policies using the robot's own experience, increasing average success percentage of single-task policies from 36% to 86% and of a pre-trained VLA from 38% to 76% while reducing the number of inference steps per action generation by 70%.
openreview:uNi5VigrGr.authors: Andreas Sochopoulos, Esmeralda S. Whitammer, Nikolaos Tsagkas, Joao Moura, Michael Gienger, Sethu Vijayakumar

openreview:uKRtsLLqs6.title: MoDex: Towards Universal Multi-Object Dexterous Grasping
openreview:uKRtsLLqs6.abstract: Multi-object grasping is a fundamental yet challenging problem, constrained by data collection costs, varying spatial layouts, and the need for broad generalization. To address these challenges, we propose MoDex, a data-efficient framework that provides the first unified solution for universal multi-object dexterous grasping across diverse spatial layouts. MoDex accomplishes this by formulating the task as a single-step decision problem of learning residual corrections to a reference trajectory, and introducing a spatially adaptive dual-strategy that performs single-shot grasping for proximal objects and sequential interaction for separated objects. Extensive evaluations show that MoDex significantly outperforms baselines in proximal configurations, achieving 64.17% success on unseen objects, and uniquely succeeds in separated layouts where prior methods struggle. Further experiments demonstrate its generalization across robot embodiments, scalability and zero-shot sim-to-real deployment through a vision-based policy trained solely on simulation data.
openreview:uKRtsLLqs6.authors: Jing Xiong, Jiale Xie, Haoqi Yuan, Chaoyi Xu, Zongqing Lu

openreview:uHhNEb0OSW.title: Barrier-Constrained Guidance For Real-time Asynchronous VLA Execution
openreview:uHhNEb0OSW.abstract: While asynchronous execution enables VLA models to operate in real-time environments by predicting the next chunk during execution, it inevitably introduces boundary misalignment with the committed action stream. Existing delay-aware solutions address this at the prohibitive cost of extensive retraining, architectural modifications, or fixed-prefix inpainting that inflates computation when low latency is vital. To address these problems, we propose FreeBar, a training-free real-time inference plugin that enables robust asynchronous execution with only marginal additional inference cost by casting chunk alignment in flow-based VLAs as barrier-guided action-space constraint. Specifically, FreeBar introduces a lightweight Control Barrier Function (CBF)-inspired consistency constraint between consecutive action chunks and solves the resulting correction in closed form, avoiding costly backpropagation through the VLA action head. By progressively tightening the consistency bound during generation, FreeBar aligns generated chunks with the committed execution stream while preserving early-stage generative flexibility and long-horizon adaptability. Across Kinetix, RoboCasa, and diverse real-world robotic platforms with multiple VLA backbones, FreeBar improves success rates over naive asynchronous execution by 10%--15% on average, with larger gains in highly dynamic scenarios. It also preserves real-time computational efficiency, decreasing inference latency per action chunk over 45% than RTC. Additionally, as a universal plugin, FreeBar remains robust across distinct latency environments, base policies, and hyperparameter settings.
openreview:uHhNEb0OSW.authors: Wenbo Yu, Jifan Li, Wenke Xia, Yuchen Li, Yizhuo Zhang, Pei Ren, Zhengping Che, Di Hu

openreview:u2dtQWAFQo.title: CA-GMT: Contact-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation of Motion Tracking for Whole-Body Teleoperation
openreview:u2dtQWAFQo.abstract: General Motion Tracking (GMT) controllers have advanced humanoid whole-body teleoperation, yet inconsistent foot-ground contact remains a recurring deployment artifact, appearing as foot skating, dragging, and mistimed transitions. Standard kinematic metrics do not fully capture this physical gap, and adapting a frozen GMT backbone to contact-sensitive failures creates a retention--adaptation trade-off shaped by the adaptation parameterization. We study this trade-off through controlled comparisons of full fine-tuning, additive residual adaptation, and low-rank updates under matched supervision and budget, and instantiate the resulting insight in Contact-Aware General Motion Tracking (CA-GMT). CA-GMT combines foot contact-grounded rewards with a low-rank update of a frozen GMT backbone, and includes a phase-conditional variant that restricts adaptation to swing frames. On a held-out evaluation corpus, CA-GMT reduces the False Contact Rate (FCR) from 0.401 to 0.235, while lowering tracking error by 16% and jerkiness by 37%. The phase-conditional variant further reduces FCR to 0.199 while remaining within the base policy's pre-training-distribution variance. Retention analysis across PT/FT/ID/OOD splits shows that the evaluated low-rank parameterization preserves out-of-distribution tracking better than the full fine-tuning and residual variants tested in this work. On a Unitree~G1, the phase-conditional variant again achieves the lowest hardware FCR.
openreview:u2dtQWAFQo.authors: Sang-Hun Kim, Hanbyel Cho, Sunkyum yoo, Donghan Koo

openreview:tsWZwXGz5P.title: AdvDex: Learning Dexterous Manipulation from Human Demonstrations via Joint-Aligned Actions and Adversarial Learning
openreview:tsWZwXGz5P.abstract: Dexterous manipulation remains a fundamental capability for embodied intelligence, yet its scalability is severely bottlenecked by expensive data acquisition and hardware fragmentation. The current ecosystem lacks a unified data paradigm, preventing the aggregation of demonstrations across structurally diverse robotic platforms. Furthermore, shared visuomotor policies often suffer from visual entanglement, where task-critical spatial semantics are confounded with embodiment-specific appearances. To overcome these barriers, we present AdvDex, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework for scalable cross-embodiment dexterous manipulation. First, we introduce OmniShare, a massive multimodal human demonstration dataset that provides high-fidelity priors to bypass teleoperation bottlenecks. Second, we propose the Joint-Aligned Action Space (JAAS), a canonical $SE(3)$ wrist and 15-finger-joint representation that seamlessly harmonizes human hands, dexterous robotic hands, and parallel grippers. Finally, we employ domain-adversarial learning to explicitly decouple embodiment-specific visual features from universal task skills. Extensive physical experiments demonstrate that AdvDex consistently outperforms single-embodiment baselines, enabling robust zero-shot policy transfer and rapid few-shot adaptation across heterogeneous hardware and unseen environments.
openreview:tsWZwXGz5P.authors: Zhiyue Zhao, Jingyi Wu, Hairuo Liu, Mingyu Liu, Liyang Li, Hengdi ZHANG, Tong He, Zhengxue Cheng

openreview:trTMmn2U1g.title: ZeroWBC: Learning Natural Whole-Body Humanoid Interaction from Human Egocentric Data
openreview:trTMmn2U1g.abstract: Achieving versatile and natural whole-body humanoid interaction control remains challenging due to the high cost of whole-body teleoperation data. We present ZeroWBC, a teleoperation-free framework that learns humanoid whole-body interaction from human egocentric videos paired with synchronized whole-body motion and text annotations. ZeroWBC adopts a generation-then-tracking formulation to tackle the static scene whole-body interaction control problem. Given an initial egocentric image and a language instruction, a fine-tuned Vision-Language Model generates future human whole-body motion tokens, which are decoded into continuous motions and retargeted to the humanoid. The resulting reference motions, together with root and key body-part trajectories, are then executed by a general interactive motion tracking policy. To improve interaction performance, we introduce an interaction-oriented tracking reward that prioritizes global root and key body-part trajectory alignment while preserving natural whole-body motion. Experiments on Unitree G1 humanoid robot show that ZeroWBC enables diverse scene-aware behaviors without robot teleoperation demonstrations. These results suggest a scalable paradigm for learning natural humanoid whole-body interaction from human egocentric data.
openreview:trTMmn2U1g.authors: Haoran Yang, Jiacheng Bao, Yucheng Xin, Haoming Song, Yuyang Tian, Bin Zhao, Dong Wang, Xuelong Li

openreview:thG2jwuii6.title: RoboPocket: Improve Robot Policies Instantly with Your Phone
openreview:thG2jwuii6.abstract: Scaling robot learning is bottlenecked not only by data volume, but also by whether the data targets the policy's failures. Existing robot-free handheld interfaces enable portable in-the-wild data collection, yet remain open-loop: users record demonstrations without feedback from the current policy. Interactive methods such as DAgger provide such feedback by collecting corrective on-policy data, but require deploying imperfect policies on physical robots, making them costly, unsafe, and difficult to scale. We present \textbf{RoboPocket}, a smartphone-based system for \textit{robot-free policy iteration}. By combining on-device sensing, display, and communication with cloud-side policy inference, RoboPocket provides real-time collection guidance and visualizes the policy's predicted trajectory in augmented reality as \textit{AR Visual Foresight}. This allows users to identify policy weaknesses and collect targeted corrective data without deploying a physical robot. An asynchronous finetuning pipeline continuously incorporates new corrections and updates the policy within minutes, realizing a DAgger-inspired robot-free correction loop. Across diverse real-world manipulation tasks, we validate RoboPocket as a scalable data engine and show that online corrective data collection achieves an average 2$\times$ sample-efficiency gain over blindly scaling offline demonstrations.
openreview:thG2jwuii6.authors: Junjie Fang, Wendi Chen, Han Xue, Fangyuan Zhou, Tian Le, Yi Wang, Yuting Zhang, Jun Lv, Chuan Wen, Cewu Lu

openreview:tfC6LMD02z.title: Proxy Policy Steering
openreview:tfC6LMD02z.abstract: Robotics foundation models carry broad manipulation priors from large-scale data, but specializing them to a new task remains the deployment bottleneck. This requires injecting new task-specific behavior from limited demonstrations without eroding their broad capabilities. We introduce Proxy Policy Steering (PPS), a novel adaptation method that addresses this challenge by training two lightweight proxy policies. A reference proxy models the frozen base's behavior on target-task observations, and a task proxy, initialized from the reference, captures how this behavior changes under task supervision. Their difference forms a calibrated velocity-space residual that steers the frozen base sampler at every denoising step. We identify the conditions under which this residual isolates the change induced by task supervision, and validate them empirically. On 8 real-world and 4 simulation manipulation tasks, PPS lifts the state-of-the-art $\pi_{0.5}$ base policy by 53% absolute success rate on average, with 0-to-1 gains on tasks the base never solves, while preserving the base's broad capabilities. PPS outperforms LoRA fine-tuning, from-scratch specialists, residual policies, and prior inference-time steering methods.
openreview:tfC6LMD02z.authors: Chuanruo Ning, Tianrui Wang, Wei-Chiu Ma, Kuan Fang

openreview:tegLlXBRCU.title: Coarse-to-Control: Action-Token Planning for Vision-Language-Action Models
openreview:tegLlXBRCU.abstract: Most vision-language-action (VLA) models map observations directly to actions without explicit intermediate planning, which limits performance on long-horizon tasks where early mistakes compound. We propose Coarse-to-Control, a plan-execute VLA that introduces planning natively in the action-token space. The key idea is to let the policy first predict a compact sequence of coarse action tokens that summarize the intended future trajectory, and then generate executable action tokens conditioned on this plan. Because both planning and execution share a unified discrete action vocabulary, the plan stays close to the control manifold and provides directly actionable guidance rather than an abstract hint that must be translated back to motor commands. Experiments on LIBERO, SimplerEnv-WidowX, and real-world manipulation tasks show that action-token planning consistently improves over direct action generation, with the largest gains on long-horizon multi-stage tasks.
openreview:tegLlXBRCU.authors: Jinhao wu, Shiduo Zhang, Yicheng Liu, Xiaopeng Yu, Sixian Li, Siyin Wang, Hang Zhao, Jingjing Gong, Xipeng Qiu

openreview:tXUfbhgQg2.title: Learning Unions of Convex Sets via Invertible Latent Decomposition for Path Planning
openreview:tXUfbhgQg2.abstract: Collision-free path planning in cluttered, real-world environments relies on a representation of the collision-free space, and existing representations broadly fall into two categories. Explicit representations, such as unions of convex sets, can be plugged into optimization-based planners as hard collision-free constraints, but their parameters scale poorly with configuration-space dimension. Implicit representations, by contrast, are flexible and scale well to complex geometries, yet typically lack such guarantees. We bridge this gap with ILD (Invertible Latent Decomposition), a framework that jointly learns an invertible mapping and a union of explicit convex polytopes in the resulting latent space. Planning is carried out over these latent convex sets, and the invertible mapping decodes the resulting paths back to the original configuration space while preserving feasibility with respect to the refined explicit safe regions. We further propose Visibility-Guided Sampling (VGS) to keep the convex sets connected for path planning. Across 2D navigation, 6-DoF, and 14-DoF manipulation environments, ILD achieves broader coverage, better inter-set connectivity, and higher path-planning success rates than prior baselines, with zero observed false positives after test-time refinement. On a 14-DoF bimanual manipulator, we further demonstrate real-time collision-free planning, with test-time refinement adapting to scene-geometry changes during real-world deployment on a single 6-DoF arm.
openreview:tXUfbhgQg2.authors: Taerim Yoon, Dongho Kang, Kisang Park, Junha Cha, Stelian Coros, Sungjoon Choi

openreview:tJpI5D27wh.title: PTLD: Sim-to-Real Privileged Tactile Latent Distillation for dexterous manipulation
openreview:tJpI5D27wh.abstract: Tactile dexterous manipulation is essential to human manipulation, yet learning effective tactile enabled robot policies remains a challenge. While recent work relies on imitation learning, obtaining high quality demonstrations for multi-fingered hands via robot tele-operation or kinesthetic teaching is prohibitive.  Alternatively, with reinforcement learning (RL) we can learn skills in simulation, but the lack of fast and realistic tactile simulation remains a core issue. To bridge this gap, we introduce sim-to-real Privileged Tactile Latent Distillation (\ourmethod). Our method anchors sim-to-real transfer on privileged sensors and learns a tactile encoder that maps real-world touch into the latent state of the privileged simulation policy, bypassing tactile simulation entirely. We demonstrate that \ourmethod improves over proprioceptive manipulation policies trained in simulation significantly by incorporating tactile sensing. On the benchmark in-hand rotation task, \ourmethod achieves a 182\% improvement. \ourmethod also enables the challenging task of tactile in-hand reorientation where we see a 57\% improvement in number of goals reached.
openreview:tJpI5D27wh.authors: Rosy Chen, Mustafa Mukadam, Michael Kaess, Tingfan Wu, Francois Robert Hogan, Jitendra Malik, Akash Sharma

openreview:tAXtXe4Oqd.title: Object-Centric Residual RL for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real VLA Enhancement
openreview:tAXtXe4Oqd.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can generalize across diverse manipulation tasks, but their imitation-learning-based policies remain brittle in precise physical interactions due to compounding execution errors; Can a reinforcement learning policy trained purely in simulation improve the robustness of real-world VLAs zero-shot? Residual RL, which learns a corrective policy on top of a frozen VLA, offers a natural framework, but existing approaches face a fundamental sim-to-real dilemma: privileged-state methods require lossy distillation for deployment; image-based methods suffer from the visual domain gap; and real-world RL is costly and unsafe. We propose an object-centric residual RL framework that refines VLA actions using object poses, enabling a compact observation space that transfers consistently between simulation and reality. To align the two domains, we additionally replay the same teleoperation demonstrations in simulation to train a sim counterpart of the real-world VLA. The residual RL policy is trained only in simulation with pose noise injection and dropout, and transfers zero-shot to the real. Across five manipulation tasks on a real Franka robot, our method improves success from 42% to 76% zero-shot, and the improved rollouts can be further reused to retrain the base VLA for self-improvement without additional teleoperation.
openreview:tAXtXe4Oqd.authors: Kinam Kim, Namiko Saito, Heecheol Kim, Katsushi Ikeuchi, Jaegul Choo, Yasuyuki Matsushita

openreview:suRtJLXVxI.title: Dex-X: Learning Visual-Tactile Dexterous Manipulation From Human Demonstration with Simulated Interaction
openreview:suRtJLXVxI.abstract: Human videos are an abundant source of dexterous manipulation behaviors, but they lack tactile information that is crucial for contact-rich interaction. This raises a fundamental question: can robots learn deployable visual-tactile dexterous manipulation policies directly from human video demonstrations? We present Dex-X, a framework for learning visual-tactile dexterous manipulation from human videos through simulation. Our key insight is that simulation can serve as a tactile completion engine. Given monocular human demonstrations, Dex-X reconstructs hand-object interactions in simulation, where physically grounded contact dynamics provide tactile supervision unavailable in the original videos. Leveraging this recovered tactile information, we train visual-tactile dexterous manipulation policies and distill them into deployable policies operating on point-cloud observations and tactile sensing. We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on dexterous hand-arm platforms across diverse grasping and contact-rich tool-use tasks.  The teacher policy achieves 65.9% average success across eight tasks in simulation, while the distilled visual-tactile policy achieves a 53% success rate on cube picking and 23% on the challenging real-world table-cleaning task, which is not achieved by existing general sim-to-real manipulation systems. Our results suggest that tactile completion is a critical ingredient for scalable dexterous manipulation learning and provide a path toward learning real-world robot skills from Internet-scale human video data.
openreview:suRtJLXVxI.authors: Ruoqu Chen, Feixiang Ruan, Liu Cao, Zihao Wang, Botian Xu, Shiqin Tong, Jiajun Liu, Wanli Xing, Kaifeng Zhang, Mengdi Xu

openreview:sitHOFsi2x.title: Do as I Do: Dexterous Manipulation Data from Everyday Human Videos
openreview:sitHOFsi2x.abstract: How can we scalably generate data for robotic manipulation, especially on human-like platforms such as dexterous multi-fingered hands? Learning from watching human videos has recently emerged as a likely answer to this question. However, difficulties in estimating hand-object interaction and crossing the human-to-robot embodiment gap have hindered the adoption of abundant monocular RGB-only human videos as the primary source of robot manipulation data. In this work, we present Do as I Do, an algorithm to reconstruct and retarget monocular RGB human videos to multi-fingered dexterous robotic hands. Do as I Do reconstructs hand-object interactions from various egocentric and exocentric in-the-wild video sources. Do as I Do then retargets these hand-object interaction estimates into a sequence of actions executable in the real world, yielding robot-complete manipulation data from disparate human videos. Overall, Do as I Do outperforms previous state of the art in estimating hand-object interactions and extracting dexterous manipulation trajectories from RGB videos, as we show on experiments on datasets with ground truths and on a dataset of video clips collected online. Finally, our experiments enable us to propose an efficacy playbook for practitioners collecting human data for manipulation.
openreview:sitHOFsi2x.authors: Bhawna Paliwal, Haritheja Etukuru, William Liang, Pieter Abbeel, Nur Muhammad Mahi Shafiullah, Jitendra Malik

openreview:sdujBb3P4e.title: FlashDrive:  Flash Vision-Language-Action Inference Framework for Autonomous Driving
openreview:sdujBb3P4e.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise to bring end-to-end reasoning to autonomous driving, but their computational cost is orders of magnitude too high for real-time control. The core challenge is that VLA inference is not a single bottleneck but a pipeline of four stages (visual encoding, language model prefilling, reasoning-token decoding, and flow-matching action prediction), each dominated by a different source of inefficiency: spatial redundancy in overlapping video frames, autoregressive serialization of reasoning chains, and over-computation in iterative denoising. Addressing any one stage in isolation leaves the others untouched. We propose FlashDrive, an algorithm-system co-design framework that targets all four stages simultaneously. A key insight is that each bottleneck admits a distinct, lightweight algorithmic shortcut: temporal overlap enables streaming KV-cache reuse across frames; the low entropy of domain-specific reasoning tokens makes them amenable to diffusion-based speculative decoding; and the non-uniform structure of the denoising velocity field, sharp at the endpoints but nearly constant in the middle, permits adaptive step caching that concentrates compute where it matters. Layered on top of system-level CUDA Graph compilation and kernel fusion, these techniques compound multiplicatively. Applied to Alpamayo1.5-10B with W4A8 quantization, \method reduces end-to-end latency from 716~ms to 159~ms (4.5x) with negligible accuracy loss (~0.07m on minADE6@6.4s and ADE@6.4s even improves), bringing VLA-driven autonomous driving to real-time viability on consumer-level GPUs.
openreview:sdujBb3P4e.authors: Zekai Li, Yihao Liang, Hongfei Zhang, Jian Chen, Yesheng Liang, Zhijian Liu

openreview:sIe2LX2HaF.title: DexNinja: Learning Robust Dexterous Cutting Policy with a Real-to-Sim-to-Real Data Engine
openreview:sIe2LX2HaF.abstract: Cutting a piece of food looks effortless in human hands: we nudge the blade, adjust the angle, modulate pressure as the skin yields and cuts. For a robot, however, every cut is a high-contact interaction with a deformable, elasto-plastic object whose behavior changes with pose, contact mode, and cutting stage. Collecting real-world data is also inherently expensive and wasteful: each trial typically contaminates, damages, or destroys the food, so obtaining scalable real world data for dexterous cutting are expensive and difficult. Simulation is an appealing alternative, but a large sim-to-real gap exists in both physics and perception. This gap is especially severe for topology-changing interactions like cutting, where small errors in contact, friction, or material and elastic transformations response quickly compound. We propose DexNinja, a differentiable real2sim2real framework that turns a handful of real demonstrations into a dense and realistic training distribution. DexNinja (i) reconstructs object instances from real trajectories, (ii) randomizes physically meaningful parameters (e.g., mass, geometry, friction) under category-level constraints, and (iii) augmented dexterous manipulation episodes using a custom differentiable simulator that couples robot dynamics, tactile contact, and deformable cutting. We evaluate DexNinja on a dexterous food-slicing task show that (1) the augmented data consistently improves sim-to-real transfer, and (2) the resulting policies generalize to out-of-distribution objects such as strawberries with varying shapes and sizes.
openreview:sIe2LX2HaF.authors: Haozhe Lou, Runyi Yang, Wanqi Zhong, Caiyun Liu, Yicheng Liu, Wenhao Liu, Wenlong Ma, Jiawei Xia, Kanzhi Wu, Danda Pani Paudel, Luc Van Gool, Hang Zhao, Yiming Li

openreview:sF3YZbbTNX.title: VoLo: A Physical Orchestrator for Open-Vocabulary Long-Horizon Manipulation
openreview:sF3YZbbTNX.abstract: Open-vocabulary long-horizon manipulation requires robots to reason over flexible instructions and complex multi-object scenes while adaptively planning, executing, monitoring, and recovering from failures. We address these demands with a closed agent loop in which a VLM orchestrates heterogeneous robot capabilities as interruptible tools. Unlike in virtual AI agents, the timing of decisions, actions and tool calls is important in a physical world that does not pause for reasoning. We refer to this setting as Physical Orchestration, and propose VoLoAgent, a VLM that plans, monitors, and recovers by treating a VLA/WAM as an interruptible tool it steers mid-rollout, complemented by vision models and action primitives. To evaluate these long-horizon capabilities, we introduce RoboVoLo, a high-fidelity benchmark for open-vocabulary long-horizon manipulation across common sense, memory/state tracking, complex references, and world knowledge, with both task-level success and failure-mode diagnostics. Experiments show VoLoAgent substantially outperforms single VLA/VLM or tool-based systems, with validation on real-robot experiments.
openreview:sF3YZbbTNX.authors: Siyi Chen, Hugo Hadfield, Alex Zook, Mikaela Angelina Uy, Chan Hee Song, Erwin Coumans, Xuning Yang, Faisal Ladhak, Qing Qu, Stan Birchfield, Jonathan Tremblay, Valts Blukis

openreview:s8ZiyIAn3z.title: Self-play is not enough: human imitation improves self-play autonomy in the wild
openreview:s8ZiyIAn3z.abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning at scale has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training autonomous driving policies, producing agents that exhibit robust collision-avoidance and stable navigation in simulation. However, policies trained purely through self-play lack exposure to the distribution of real human driving behavior, resulting in trajectories that appear unnatural. To overcome this, we present Self-play with Human Imitation Fine-Tuning (SHIFT), a hybrid training framework that fine-tunes a pretrained self-play foundation policy on real-world driving demonstrations without changing the underlying reinforcement learning algorithm. SHIFT fine-tunes in closed-loop log-replay simulation, in which the ego vehicle is rolled out by the learned policy while the non-ego agents are replayed from logged human trajectories. Distance to the human expert trajectory is simply an additional reward term in the same PPO with advantage filtering algorithm used for pretraining. To enable extended fine-tuning without losing the base self-play performance, we use a KL regularization loss against the frozen self-play foundation policy. On the closed-loop nuPlan Val14 benchmark, SHIFT improves over the self-play baseline in human-likeness (ADE: 9.4 m → 8.0 m, FDE: 21.3 m → 18.5 m), safety (collision rate: 6.4% → 3.9%, drivable area violations: 2.5% → 1.7%, red light violations: 1.6% → 1.0%), and comfort (brake tap rate: 29% → 20%, oscillation rate: 9% → 4%), and achieves the best ADE, FDE, collision, and drivable area scores among all baselines, including extended self-play, behavior cloning, BC+RL, and human-regularized PPO. We deploy both policies on self-driving cars and find similar improvements in the real world (2.6× fewer safety takeovers: one every 0.57 → 1.46 miles). To our knowledge, this is the first evaluation of self-play and self-play with human imitation on public roads. Our results suggest that post-training self-play with human imitation, stabilized by KL regularization, is a promising direction for deployable autonomous driving systems. An open-source implementation, along with additional materials, will be available on the project page: https://rohit-ash.github.io/SHIFT/
openreview:s8ZiyIAn3z.authors: Marc Heim, Bassam Helou, Rohit Satishkumar, Momchil Tomov, Hansford C. Hendargo, Nicolas Rey, Gianmarco Bernasconi, Joseph Baker, Alexander Boule, Rafael DaSilva, Abed Ghanbari, Cedric Warny, Yi Huo, Phuc Xuan Nguyen, Neset Unver Akmandor, Sarjak Thakkar, Daphne Cornelisse, Eugene Vinitsky, Forbes Howington, Boaz Floor, Yiluan Guo, Samuel Findler, Sourabh Vora

openreview:rfRjWMFfvV.title: Sequential Asymmetric Imitation for Learning Coupled Robot Policies
openreview:rfRjWMFfvV.abstract: Collaborative mobile manipulation requires robots to coordinate with a partially observed partner while physically interacting through shared objects. This is difficult because failures often arise not from poor local skills, but from mistimed waiting, yielding, pulling, releasing, or repositioning. We study this problem with two bimanual mobile manipulators coupled through rigid and deformable objects. We propose Sequential Asymmetric Imitation (SAI), a single-teleoperator curriculum for learning coupled multi-robot behaviors without synchronized dual-operator demonstrations or explicit inter-robot communication. SAI trains Robot A from unilateral demonstrations with a compliant human partner, trains Robot B against the deployed Robot A policy, and then refines Robot A using sparse interventions near coordination failures. This staged process exposes the policies to increasingly realistic partner behaviors, including delay, phase mismatch, insufficient yielding, and interaction conflict. Across real-world dual-robot manipulation tasks, SAI improves task success, phase synchronization, and partner-contingent yielding over independent imitation and curriculum-ablation baselines. These results suggest that physically coupled collaboration can be learned through the structure of the imitation curriculum, rather than through synchronized multi-operator demonstrations or explicit coordination mechanisms.
openreview:rfRjWMFfvV.authors: Ranpeng Qiu, Yincong Chen, Zihao Li, Yanan Zhou, Guoqiang Ren, Weiming Zhi

openreview:rcE4amkjBq.title: GeoProp: Grounding Robot State in Vision for Generalist Manipulation
openreview:rcE4amkjBq.abstract: Proprioception is fundamental to robotic manipulation, yet standard fusion methods often treat it as an isolated vector lacking explicit alignment with visual tokens. Without a direct correspondence between 3D kinematics and 2D feature maps, manipulation policies struggle to ground the robot’s state within the scene, frequently underperforming even vision-only baselines. To address this, we introduce GeoProp, a lightweight, plug-and-play adapter that aligns proprioception with vision through explicit geometric grounding and spatial feature sampling. GeoProp projects the robot state onto the image plane to sample localized visual features, constructing a grounded state token. It then injects state-derived spatial priors into the corresponding visual features via FiLM modulation. To capture motion intent, GeoProp further samples features at a short-horizon predicted coordinate derived from kinematic velocity, providing look-ahead visual context. Across 67 tasks, GeoProp improves success rates by 9.4% in simulation and 11.2% in the real world, while adding only 3% to the parameter count. These results demonstrate that explicitly resolving state–vision misalignment is a simple yet high-impact inductive bias for generalist embodied policies.
openreview:rcE4amkjBq.authors: Guoyang Zhao, Quanhao Qian, Gongjie Zhang, Wenhao Li, Jiuniu Wang, Xiaowei Lu, Deli Zhao, Ran Xu

openreview:rYkaehgzzO.title: See Less, Specify More: Visual Evidence Budgets for Generalizable VLAs
openreview:rYkaehgzzO.abstract: Generalization remains a central bottleneck for vision-language-action (VLA) models: under distractors, appearance shifts, and semantically similar tasks, the policy must often infer local execution details from coarse instructions while also deciding which parts of the image matter for control. We present S2 (See Less, Specify More), a framework for improving VLA generalization by training the executor under a cleaner interface.  Specify More preserves the original instruction as a stable high-level goal while relabeling each trajectory into refined trajectory- and subtask-level language that disambiguates the current execution mode. Unlike native attention, See Less imposes an explicit visual evidence budget, training the executor to act from task-sufficient evidence rather than unconstrained visual context, without any region or mask annotation.  This interface lets the executor follow detailed guidance without relying on distracting visual patches or resolving avoidable ambiguity on its own, and it remains compatible with off-the-shelf VLM planners through in-context learning.
